passages.vernacularMandarin: 『噓!我的漂亮寶貝,』他說,『站著別動,站著別動。』

passages.original: His very voice did me good, and the bathing was very comfortable.
passages.vernacular: 佢嘅聲音本身就讓我好受,洗澡都好舒服。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他的聲音本身就讓我好受,洗澡也很舒服。

passages.original: The skin was so broken at the corners of my mouth that I could not eat the hay, the stalks hurt me.
passages.vernacular: 我嘴角嘅皮破得好厲害,我食不咗乾草,草莖弄疼我。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我嘴角的皮破得很厲害,我吃不了乾草,草莖弄疼我。

passages.original: He looked closely at it, shook his head, and told the man to fetch a good bran mash and put some meal into it.
passages.vernacular: 佢仔細睇咗睇,搖搖頭,叫嗰人去攞一份好嘅麩皮糊,放些粗粉進去。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他仔細看了看,搖搖頭,叫那人去拿一份好的麩皮糊,放些粗粉進去。

passages.original: How good that mash was! and so soft and healing to my mouth.
passages.vernacular: 嗰糊幾咁好食啊!對我嘅嘴咁柔軟、有療效。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那糊多麼好吃啊!對我的嘴那麼柔軟、有療效。

passages.original: He stood by all the time I was eating, stroking me and talking to the man.
passages.vernacular: 我食嘅時候佢一直站喺旁邊,撫摸我,同嗰人講話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我吃的時候他一直站在旁邊,撫摸我,同那人說話。

passages.original: 'If a high-mettled creature like this,' said he, 'can't be broken by fair means, she will never be good for anything.'
passages.vernacular: 『如果像咁樣一個烈性嘅生靈,』佢講,『唔能夠用公正嘅辦法馴服,佢將永遠唔會成器。』
passages.vernacularMandarin: 『如果像這樣一個烈性的生靈,』他說,『不能用公正的辦法馴服,她將永遠不會成器。』

passages.original: “After that he often came to see me, and when my mouth was healed the other breaker, Job, they called him, went on training me; he was steady and thoughtful, and I soon learned what he wanted.”
passages.vernacular: 「此後佢常嚟睇我,等我嘅嘴癒合喇,另一個馴馬人,佢哋叫佢喬布,繼續訓練我;佢沉穩,想得周到,我好快就明白咗佢要乜嘢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「此後他常來看我,等我的嘴癒合了,另一個馴馬人,他們叫他喬布,繼續訓練我;他沉穩,想得周到,我很快就明白了他要什麼。」

chapters.title: Part I · 08 Ginger's Story Continued 第一部·08 金姐的故事(續)

passages.original: CH The next time that Ginger and I were together in the paddock she told me about her first place.
passages.vernacular: 下一次金姐同我一起喺牧場上時,佢告訴我佢嘅第一個地方。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 下一次金姐和我一起在牧場上時,她告訴我她的第一個地方。

passages.original: “After my breaking in,” she said, “I was bought by a dealer to match another chestnut horse.
passages.vernacular: 「我被馴服之後,」佢講,「被一個商人買去,配另一匹栗色馬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我被馴服之後,」她說,「被一個商人買去,配另一匹栗色馬。

passages.original: For some weeks he drove us together, and then we were sold to a fashionable gentleman, and were sent up to London.
passages.vernacular: 好幾個星期佢讓我哋一起拉車,然後我哋被賣畀咗一位時髦嘅先生,被送到咗倫敦。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 好幾個星期他讓我們一起拉車,然後我們被賣給了一位時髦的先生,被送到了倫敦。

passages.original: I had been driven with a check-rein by the dealer, and I hated it worse than anything else; but in this place we were reined far tighter, the coachman and his master thinking we looked more stylish so.
passages.vernacular: 商人畀我套住止韁繩駕車,我恨佢超過一切;不過喺呢個地方我哋被勒得緊得多,車夫同佢嘅主人認為咁樣我哋睇起嚟更有派頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 商人給我套著止韁繩駕車,我恨它超過一切;可是在這個地方我們被勒得緊得多,車夫和他的主人認為這樣我們看起來更有派頭。

passages.original: We were often driven about in the park and other fashionable places.
passages.vernacular: 我哋常被駕住喺公園同其他時髦嘅地方轉。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們常被駕著在公園和其他時髦的地方轉。

passages.original: You who never had a check-rein on don't know what it is, but I can tell you it is dreadful.
passages.vernacular: 你哋從冇戴過止韁繩嘅,唔知道嗰個係乜嘢,但我可以告訴你,嗰好可怕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你們從沒戴過止韁繩的,不知道那是什麼,但我可以告訴你,那很可怕。

passages.original: “I like to toss my head about and hold it as high as any horse; but fancy now yourself, if you tossed your head up high and were obliged to hold it there, and that for hours together, not able to move it at all, except with a jerk still higher, your neck aching till you did not know how to bear it.
passages.vernacular: 「我鍾意甩頭,像任何馬一樣把佢抬得高高嘅;不過你而家想像一下,如果你把頭高高揚起,而且唔得不一直嗰樣抬住,一連幾個小時,完全唔能夠動,除咗猛地抬得更高,你嘅脖子痛得讓你唔知點忍受。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我喜歡甩頭,像任何馬一樣把它抬得高高的;可是你現在想像一下,如果你把頭高高揚起,而且不得不一直那樣抬著,一連幾個小時,完全不能動,除了猛地抬得更高,你的脖子痛得讓你不知怎麼忍受。

passages.original: Besides that, to have two bits instead of one--and mine was a sharp one, it hurt my tongue and my jaw, and the blood from my tongue colored the froth that kept flying from my lips as I chafed and fretted at the bits and rein.
passages.vernacular: 此外,仲要有兩個嚼子,而唔係一個——我嘅一個仲好尖利,佢弄痛我嘅舌頭同下顎,舌頭上嘅血染紅咗我因為對嚼子同韁繩惱怒煩躁而不斷從嘴唇飛出嘅泡沫。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 此外,還要有兩個嚼子,而不是一個——我的一個還很尖利,它弄痛我的舌頭和下顎,舌頭上的血染紅了我因為對嚼子和韁繩惱怒煩躁而不斷從嘴唇飛出的泡沫。

passages.original: It was worst when we had to stand by the hour waiting for our mistress at some grand party or entertainment, and if I fretted or stamped with impatience the whip was laid on.
passages.vernacular: 最糟嘅係,我哋必須喺某個盛大嘅聚會或娛樂活動前,一等就係好幾個小時,等我哋嘅女主人,而如果我因為不耐煩而煩躁或跺腳,鞭子就會抽下嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 最糟的是,我們必須在某個盛大的聚會或娛樂活動前,一等就是好幾個小時,等我們的女主人,而如果我因為不耐煩而煩躁或跺腳,鞭子就會抽下來。

passages.original: It was enough to drive one mad.”
passages.vernacular: 呢足以把人逼瘋。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這足以把人逼瘋。」

passages.original: “Did not your master take any thought for you?”
passages.vernacular: 「你嘅主人就冇為你著想嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你的主人就沒有為你著想嗎?」

passages.original: I said.
passages.vernacular: 我講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我說。

passages.original: “No,” said she, “he only cared to have a stylish turnout, as they call it; I think he knew very little about horses; he left that to his coachman, who told him I had an irritable temper! that I had not been well broken to the check-rein, but I should soon get used to it; but he was not the man to do it, for when I was in the stable, miserable and angry, instead of being smoothed and quieted by kindness, I got only a surly word or a blow.
passages.vernacular: 「冇,」佢講,「佢只在乎有一副時髦嘅排場,像佢哋講嘅;我想佢對馬所知甚少;佢把呢事交畀佢嘅車夫,車夫告訴佢我脾氣暴躁!講我冇被好好馴服嚟適應止韁繩,不過我好快會習慣嘅;但佢唔係做呢件事嘅人,因為我喺馬廄裡,痛苦又憤怒,冇被善意撫慰同安靜下嚟,卻只得到粗魯嘅一句話或一下打。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「沒有,」她說,「他只在乎有一副時髦的排場,像他們說的;我想他對馬所知甚少;他把這事交給他的車夫,車夫告訴他我脾氣暴躁!說我沒有被好好馴服來適應止韁繩,可是我很快會習慣的;但他不是做這件事的人,因為我在馬廄裡,痛苦又憤怒,沒有被善意撫慰和安靜下來,卻只得到粗魯的一句話或一下打。

passages.original: If he had been civil I would have tried to bear it.
passages.vernacular: 如果佢有禮貌,我會試住忍受。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 如果他有禮貌,我會試著忍受。

passages.original: I was willing to work, and ready to work hard too; but to be tormented for nothing but their fancies angered me.
passages.vernacular: 我願意幹活,都準備賣力幹活;但係為了佢哋嘅幻想而白白受折磨,激怒咗我。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我願意幹活,也準備賣力幹活;但是為了他們的幻想而白白受折磨,激怒了我。

passages.original: What right had they to make me suffer like that?
passages.vernacular: 佢哋有乜嘢權利讓我嗰樣受苦?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們有什麼權利讓我那樣受苦?

passages.original: Besides the soreness in my mouth, and the pain in my neck, it always made my windpipe feel bad, and if I had stopped there long I know it would have spoiled my breathing; but I grew more and more restless and irritable, I could not help it; and I began to snap and kick when any one came to harness me; for this the groom beat me, and one day, as they had just buckled us into the carriage, and were straining my head up with that rein, I began to plunge and kick with all my might.
passages.vernacular: 除咗嘴裡嘅疼痛同脖子嘅疼痛,佢仲總讓我嘅氣管感覺難受,如果我喺嗰度待得太久,我知道佢會毀咗我嘅呼吸;但我變得越嚟越焦躁易怒,我控制不住;每當有人嚟畀我套挽具,我就開始亂啃亂踢;為此馬夫打我,有一天,佢哋剛把我哋扣進馬車,用嗰根韁繩把我嘅頭使勁往上勒,我開始拚命猛衝亂踢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 除了嘴裡的疼痛和脖子的疼痛,它還總讓我的氣管感覺難受,如果我在那裡待得太久,我知道它會毀了我的呼吸;但我變得越來越焦躁易怒,我控制不住;每當有人來給我套挽具,我就開始亂啃亂踢;為此馬夫打我,有一天,他們剛把我們扣進馬車,用那根韁繩把我的頭使勁往上勒,我開始拚命猛衝亂踢。

passages.original: I soon broke a lot of harness, and kicked myself clear; so that was an end of that place.
passages.vernacular: 我好快弄斷咗一堆挽具,踢開咗自己;呢個就係嗰個地方嘅結局。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我很快弄斷了一堆挽具,踢開了自己;這就是那個地方的結局。

passages.original: “After this I was sent to Tattersall's to be sold; of course I could not be warranted free from vice, so nothing was said about that.
passages.vernacular: 「呢之後我被送到塔特索爾拍賣行去賣;當然我唔能夠保證冇惡習,所以冇提呢件事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這之後我被送到塔特索爾拍賣行去賣;當然我不能保證沒有惡習,所以沒提這件事。

passages.original: My handsome appearance and good paces soon brought a gentleman to bid for me, and I was bought by another dealer; he tried me in all kinds of ways and with different bits, and he soon found out what I could not bear.
passages.vernacular: 我漂亮嘅外表同好步伐好快讓一位先生出價買我,我被另一個商人買下;佢用各種辦法、各種嚼子試我,好快就發現咗我受不了乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我漂亮的外表和好步伐很快讓一位先生出價買我,我被另一個商人買下;他用各種辦法、各種嚼子試我,很快就發現了我受不了什麼。

passages.original: At last he drove me quite without a check-rein, and then sold me as a perfectly quiet horse to a gentleman in the country; he was a good master, and I was getting on very well, but his old groom left him and a new one came.
passages.vernacular: 最後佢完全唔使止韁繩駕我,然後把我當作一匹完全安靜嘅馬賣畀咗鄉下嘅一位先生;佢係個好主人,我過得好好,但佢嘅老馬夫離開咗佢,嚟咗一個新嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 最後他完全不用止韁繩駕我,然後把我當作一匹完全安靜的馬賣給了鄉下的一位先生;他是個好主人,我過得很好,但他的老馬夫離開了他,來了一個新的。

passages.original: This man was as hard-tempered and hard-handed as Samson; he always spoke in a rough, impatient voice, and if I did not move in the stall the moment he wanted me, he would hit me above the hocks with his stable broom or the fork, whichever he might have in his hand.
passages.vernacular: 呢人同參孫一樣脾氣冷酷、手勁粗硬;佢講話總是粗聲粗氣、不耐煩,如果我冇喺佢想要嘅嗰一刻喺馬棚裡移動,佢就會用佢手裡攞住嘅馬廄掃帚或叉子,打我後腿膝彎上面。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這人和參孫一樣脾氣冷酷、手勁粗硬;他說話總是粗聲粗氣、不耐煩,如果我沒有在他想要的那一刻在馬棚裡移動,他就會用他手裡拿著的馬廄掃帚或叉子,打我後腿膝彎上面。

passages.original: Everything he did was rough, and I began to hate him; he wanted to make me afraid of him, but I was too high-mettled for that, and one day when he had aggravated me more than usual I bit him, which of course put him in a great rage, and he began to hit me about the head with a riding whip.
passages.vernacular: 佢做嘅一切都粗暴,我開始恨佢;佢想讓我怕佢,不過我性子太烈,不食呢一套,有一天佢比平常更激怒我時,我咬咗佢,呢當然使佢大怒,佢開始用馬鞭抽打我嘅頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他做的一切都粗暴,我開始恨他;他想讓我怕他,可是我性子太烈,不吃這一套,有一天他比平常更激怒我時,我咬了他,這當然使他大怒,他開始用馬鞭抽打我的頭。

passages.original: After that he never dared to come into my stall again; either my heels or my teeth were ready for him, and he knew it.
passages.vernacular: 此後佢再都唔敢進我嘅馬棚;我嘅後蹄或牙齒隨時準備對付佢,佢知道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 此後他再也不敢進我的馬棚;我的後蹄或牙齒隨時準備對付他,他知道。

passages.original: I was quite quiet with my master, but of course he listened to what the man said, and so I was sold again.
passages.vernacular: 我對我嘅主人好安靜,但當然佢聽咗嗰人講嘅話,於是我又被賣喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我對我的主人很安靜,但當然他聽了那人說的話,於是我又被賣了。

passages.original: “The same dealer heard of me, and said he thought he knew one place where I should do well.
passages.vernacular: 「同一個商人聽講咗我,講佢想佢知道一個我會過得好嘅地方。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「同一個商人聽說了我,說他想他知道一個我會過得好的地方。

passages.original: ''Twas a pity,' he said, 'that such a fine horse should go to the bad, for want of a real good chance,' and the end of it was that I came here not long before you did; but I had then made up my mind that men were my natural enemies and that I must defend myself.
passages.vernacular: 『』佢講,『咁好嘅一匹馬因為缺乏真正嘅好機會而走向墮落,真可惜,』結果我就喺你嚟之前不久到咗呢度;不過嗰時我已經下定決心,人係我天生嘅敵人,我必須保護自己。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 『』他說,『這麼好的一匹馬因為缺乏真正的好機會而走向墮落,真可惜,』結果我就在你來之前不久到了這裡;不過那時我已經下定決心,人是我天生的敵人,我必須保護自己。

passages.original: Of course it is very different here, but who knows how long it will last?
passages.vernacular: 當然呢度好不一樣,不過邊個知道能持續多久?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然這裡很不一樣,可是誰知道能持續多久?

passages.original: I wish I could think about things as you do; but I can't, after all I have gone through.”
passages.vernacular: 我希望我能像你嗰樣想事情;不過經歷咗呢一切之後,我唔能夠。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我希望我能像你那樣想事情;可是經歷了這一切之後,我不能。」

passages.original: “Well,” I said, “I think it would be a real shame if you were to bite or kick John or James.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,」我講,「如果你咬或踢約翰或詹姆斯,我想嗰真係太丟人喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,」我說,「如果你咬或踢約翰或詹姆斯,我想那真是太丟人了。」

passages.original: “I don't mean to,” she said, “while they are good to me.
passages.vernacular: 「我不打算嗰樣,」佢講,「只要佢哋對我好。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不打算那樣,」她說,「只要他們對我好。

passages.original: I did bite James once pretty sharp, but John said, 'Try her with kindness,' and instead of punishing me as I expected, James came to me with his arm bound up, and brought me a bran mash and stroked me; and I have never snapped at him since, and I won't either.”
passages.vernacular: 我曾經相當狠地咬過詹姆斯一次,不過約翰講:『用善意對待佢』,詹姆斯冇像我預料嘅嗰樣懲罰我,而係胳膊綁住繃帶嚟到我身邊,畀我帶嚟麩皮糊,撫摸我;從嗰以後我再都冇對佢亂啃過,以後都唔會。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我曾經相當狠地咬過詹姆斯一次,可是約翰說:『用善意對待她』,詹姆斯沒有像我預料的那樣懲罰我,而是胳膊綁著繃帶來到我身邊,給我帶來麩皮糊,撫摸我;從那以後我再也沒有對他亂啃過,以後也不會。」

passages.original: I was sorry for Ginger, but of course I knew very little then, and I thought most likely she made the worst of it; however, I found that as the weeks went on she grew much more gentle and cheerful, and had lost the watchful, defiant look that she used to turn on any strange person who came near her; and one day James said, “I do believe that mare is getting fond of me, she quite whinnied after me this morning when I had been rubbing her forehead.”
passages.vernacular: 我為金姐難過,但當然嗰時我知道得好少,我以為佢好可能把事情講得最壞;然而,我發現隨住幾個星期過去,佢變得溫和快樂得多,失去咗佢以前對任何走近佢嘅陌生人露出嘅嗰種警惕、挑釁嘅神色;有一天詹姆斯講:「我真相信嗰匹母馬喺鍾意我,今日早晨我畀佢摩挲額頭時,佢喺我身後嘶鳴喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我為金姐難過,但當然那時我知道得很少,我以為她很可能把事情說得最壞;然而,我發現隨著幾個星期過去,她變得溫和快樂得多,失去了她以前對任何走近她的陌生人露出的那種警惕、挑釁的神色;有一天詹姆斯說:「我真相信那匹母馬在喜歡我,今天早晨我給她摩挲額頭時,她在我身後嘶鳴了。」

passages.original: “Ay, ay, Jim, 'tis 'the Birtwick balls',” said John, “she'll be as good as Black Beauty by and by; kindness is all the physic she wants, poor thing!”
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,係啊,吉姆,呢個係『伯特威克丸』,」約翰講,「佢好快會像黑神駒一樣好;善意係佢唯一需要嘅藥,可憐嘅嘢!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,是啊,吉姆,這是『伯特威克丸』,」約翰說,「她很快會像黑神駒一樣好;善意是她唯一需要的藥,可憐的東西!」

passages.original: Master noticed the change, too, and one day when he got out of the carriage and came to speak to us, as he often did, he stroked her beautiful neck.
passages.vernacular: 主人都注意到咗變化,有一天佢從馬車下嚟,像佢常做嘅嗰樣走過嚟同我哋講話,佢撫摸佢美麗嘅脖子。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 主人也注意到了變化,有一天他從馬車下來,像他常做的那樣走過來同我們說話,他撫摸她美麗的脖子。

passages.original: “Well, my pretty one, well, how do things go with you now?
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,我嘅漂亮寶貝,嗯,你而家過得點樣?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,我的漂亮寶貝,嗯,你現在過得怎麼樣?

passages.original: You are a good bit happier than when you came to us, I think.”
passages.vernacular: 我想你比剛嚟我哋呢度時開心多喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我想你比剛來我們這裡時開心多了。」

passages.original: She put her nose up to him in a friendly, trustful way, while he rubbed it gently.
passages.vernacular: 佢友好而信任地把鼻子伸向佢,佢輕輕地摩挲住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她友好而信任地把鼻子伸向他,他輕輕地摩挲著。

passages.original: “We shall make a cure of her, John,” he said.
passages.vernacular: 「我哋要治好佢,約翰,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我們要治好她,約翰,」他說。

passages.original: “Yes, sir, she's wonderfully improved; she's not the same creature that she was; it's 'the Birtwick balls', sir,” said John, laughing.
passages.vernacular: 「係嘅,先生,佢大大改善喇;佢唔再係以前嗰個樣子喇;係『伯特威克丸』,先生,」約翰笑住講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是的,先生,她大大改善了;她不再是以前那個樣子了;是『伯特威克丸』,先生,」約翰笑著說。

passages.original: This was a little joke of John's; he used to say that a regular course of “the Birtwick horseballs” would cure almost any vicious horse; these balls, he said, were made up of patience and gentleness, firmness and petting, one pound of each to be mixed up with half a pint of common sense, and given to the horse every day.
passages.vernacular: 呢個係約翰嘅一個小玩笑;佢常講,按療程食「伯特威克馬丸」,幾乎能治好任何惡癖嘅馬;佢講,呢啲丸子係用耐心同溫柔、堅定同寵愛製成嘅,每樣一磅,摻上半品脫常識,每天餵畀馬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這是約翰的一個小玩笑;他常說,按療程吃「伯特威克馬丸」,幾乎能治好任何惡癖的馬;他說,這些丸子是用耐心和溫柔、堅定和寵愛製成的,每樣一磅,摻上半品脫常識,每天餵給馬。

chapters.title: Part I · 09 Merrylegs 第一部·09 梅利萊格斯

passages.original: CH Mr. Blomefield, the vicar, had a large family of boys and girls; sometimes they used to come and play with Miss Jessie and Flora.
passages.vernacular: 牧師布洛姆菲爾德先生有一大家子男孩女孩;有時佢哋嚟同潔西小姐、弗洛拉小姐一起玩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 牧師布洛姆菲爾德先生有一大家子男孩女孩;有時他們來和潔西小姐、弗洛拉小姐一起玩。

passages.original: One of the girls was as old as Miss Jessie; two of the boys were older, and there were several little ones.
passages.vernacular: 其中一個女孩同潔西小姐一樣大;兩個男孩比佢大,仲有幾個小嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 其中一個女孩和潔西小姐一樣大;兩個男孩比她大,還有幾個小的。

passages.original: When they came there was plenty of work for Merrylegs, for nothing pleased them so much as getting on him by turns and riding him all about the orchard and the home paddock, and this they would do by the hour together.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋嚟時,梅利萊格斯有好多活要幹,因為冇乜嘢比輪流爬上佢嘅背、騎住佢滿果園同家庭牧場轉更讓佢哋高興嘅喇,佢哋可以一連幾個小時咁樣玩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們來時,梅利萊格斯有很多活要幹,因為沒有什麼比輪流爬上他的背、騎著他滿果園和家庭牧場轉更讓他們高興的了,他們可以一連幾個小時這樣玩。

passages.original: One afternoon he had been out with them a long time, and when James brought him in and put on his halter he said:
passages.vernacular: 一天下午,佢同佢哋出去咗好久,詹姆斯把佢牽回嚟,畀佢套上籠頭時講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一天下午,他同他們出去了很久,詹姆斯把他牽回來,給他套上籠頭時說:

passages.original: “There, you rogue, mind how you behave yourself, or we shall get into trouble.”
passages.vernacular: 「好喇,你呢個淘氣包,注意你嘅行為,否則我哋會惹麻煩。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「好了,你這個淘氣包,注意你的行為,否則我們會惹麻煩。」

passages.original: “What have you been doing, Merrylegs?”
passages.vernacular: 「你都幹咗乜嘢,梅利萊格斯?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你都幹了什麼,梅利萊格斯?」

passages.original: I asked.
passages.vernacular: 我問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我問。

passages.original: “Oh!” said he, tossing his little head, “I have only been giving those young people a lesson; they did not know when they had had enough, nor when I had had enough, so I just pitched them off backward; that was the only thing they could understand.”
passages.vernacular: 「哦!」佢甩住佢嘅小腦袋講,「我只係畀嗰啲年輕人上咗一課;佢哋唔知道乜嘢時候夠喇,都唔知道我乜嘢時候夠喇,所以我就把佢哋向後摔下去;嗰個係佢哋唯一能明白嘅事。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦!」他甩著他的小腦袋說,「我只是給那些年輕人上了一課;他們不知道什麼時候夠了,也不知道我什麼時候夠了,所以我就把他們向後摔下去;那是他們唯一能明白的事。」

passages.original: “What!” said I, “you threw the children off?
passages.vernacular: 「乜嘢!」我講,「你把細路哋摔下嚟喇?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「什麼!」我說,「你把孩子們摔下來了?

passages.original: I thought you did know better than that!
passages.vernacular: 我以為你比嗰懂事!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我以為你比那懂事!

passages.original: Did you throw Miss Jessie or Miss Flora?”
passages.vernacular: 你把潔西小姐或弗洛拉小姐摔下嚟咗嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你把潔西小姐或弗洛拉小姐摔下來了嗎?」

passages.original: He looked very much offended, and said:
passages.vernacular: 佢顯得好委屈,講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他顯得非常委屈,說:

passages.original: “Of course not; I would not do such a thing for the best oats that ever came into the stable; why, I am as careful of our young ladies as the master could be, and as for the little ones it is I who teach them to ride.
passages.vernacular: 「當然唔係;就係畀我送到馬廄嚟嘅最好嘅燕麥,我都唔會做咁樣嘅事;嗨,我對我哋嘅小姐哋像主人一樣小心,至於小嘅哋,係我教佢哋騎馬嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「當然不是;就是給我送到馬廄來的最好的燕麥,我也不會做這樣的事;嗨,我對我們的小姐們像主人一樣小心,至於小的們,是我教她們騎馬的。

passages.original: When they seem frightened or a little unsteady on my back I go as smooth and as quiet as old pussy when she is after a bird; and when they are all right I go on again faster, you see, just to use them to it; so don't you trouble yourself preaching to me; I am the best friend and the best riding-master those children have.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋好像害怕或喺我背上有點不穩時,我就走得像老貓追鳥時嗰樣平穩安靜;佢哋冇事時,我又走得更快,你睇,只係讓佢哋習慣;所以你別費心對我講教;我係嗰啲細路哋最好嘅朋友同最好嘅騎術教練。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她們好像害怕或在我背上有點不穩時,我就走得像老貓追鳥時那樣平穩安靜;她們沒事時,我又走得更快,你看,只是讓她們習慣;所以你別費心對我說教;我是那些孩子們最好的朋友和最好的騎術教練。

passages.original: It is not them, it is the boys; boys,” said he, shaking his mane, “are quite different; they must be broken in as we were broken in when we were colts, and just be taught what's what.
passages.vernacular: 唔係佢哋,係男孩哋;男孩,」佢甩住鬃毛講,「完全不同;佢哋必須像我哋小時候嗰樣被馴服,學學乜嘢係乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不是她們,是男孩們;男孩,」他甩著鬃毛說,「完全不同;他們必須像我們小時候那樣被馴服,學學什麼是什麼。

passages.original: The other children had ridden me about for nearly two hours, and then the boys thought it was their turn, and so it was, and I was quite agreeable.
passages.vernacular: 其他細路騎咗我將近兩個小時,然後男孩哋覺得輪到佢哋喇,確實輪到喇,我都好樂意。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 其他孩子騎了我將近兩個小時,然後男孩們覺得輪到他們了,確實輪到了,我也很樂意。

passages.original: They rode me by turns, and I galloped them about, up and down the fields and all about the orchard, for a good hour.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋輪流騎我,我帶住佢哋飛奔,喺田野裡上下,滿果園跑,足足跑咗一個小時。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們輪流騎我,我帶著他們飛奔,在田野裡上下,滿果園跑,足足跑了一個小時。

passages.original: They had each cut a great hazel stick for a riding-whip, and laid it on a little too hard; but I took it in good part, till at last I thought we had had enough, so I stopped two or three times by way of a hint.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋每人砍咗一根大榛樹枝當馬鞭,抽得有點太狠;但我好好地接受喇,直到我最後覺得夠喇,就停咗兩三次作為暗示。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們每人砍了一根大榛樹枝當馬鞭,抽得有點太狠;但我好好地接受了,直到我最後覺得夠了,就停了兩三次作為暗示。

passages.original: Boys, you see, think a horse or pony is like a steam-engine or a thrashing-machine, and can go on as long and as fast as they please; they never think that a pony can get tired, or have any feelings; so as the one who was whipping me could not understand I just rose up on my hind legs and let him slip off behind--that was all.
passages.vernacular: 你睇,男孩哋以為馬或小馬像蒸汽機或脫粒機一樣,想多久多快就能持續多久多快;佢哋從唔想小馬會累,會有感覺;所以因為抽打我嘅嗰個不明白,我就用後腿站起嚟,讓佢從後面滑下去——就係咁樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你看,男孩們以為馬或小馬像蒸汽機或脫粒機一樣,想多久多快就能持續多久多快;他們從不想小馬會累,會有感覺;所以因為抽打我的那個不明白,我就用後腿站起來,讓他從後面滑下去——就是這樣。

passages.original: He mounted me again, and I did the same.
passages.vernacular: 佢又騎上我,我又咁樣做。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他又騎上我,我又這樣做。

passages.original: Then the other boy got up, and as soon as he began to use his stick I laid him on the grass, and so on, till they were able to understand--that was all.
passages.vernacular: 然後另一個男孩上嚟,佢一開始使用佢嘅棍子,我就把佢放倒喺草地上,如此等等,直到佢哋能夠明白——就係咁樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後另一個男孩上來,他一開始使用他的棍子,我就把他放倒在草地上,如此等等,直到他們能夠明白——就是這樣。

passages.original: They are not bad boys; they don't wish to be cruel.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋唔係壞細路;佢哋唔想殘忍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們不是壞孩子;他們不想殘忍。

passages.original: I like them very well; but you see I had to give them a lesson.
passages.vernacular: 我挺鍾意佢哋;不過你睇,我必須畀佢哋上一課。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我挺喜歡他們;可是你看,我必須給他們上一課。

passages.original: When they brought me to James and told him I think he was very angry to see such big sticks.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋把我牽到詹姆斯嗰度並告訴佢時,我想佢睇到咁大嘅棍子好生氣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們把我牽到詹姆斯那裡並告訴他時,我想他看到這麼大的棍子非常生氣。

passages.original: He said they were only fit for drovers or gypsies, and not for young gentlemen.”
passages.vernacular: 佢講嗰啲只配畀趕牲口嘅或吉卜賽人用,不配畀年輕紳士用。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他說那些只配給趕牲口的或吉卜賽人用,不配給年輕紳士用。」

passages.original: “If I had been you,” said Ginger, “I would have given those boys a good kick, and that would have given them a lesson.”
passages.vernacular: 「如果我係你,」金姐講,「我會畀嗰啲男孩狠狠踢一腳,嗰才畀佢哋上咗一課。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「如果我是你,」金姐說,「我會給那些男孩狠狠踢一腳,那才給他們上了一課。」

passages.original: “No doubt you would,” said Merrylegs; “but then I am not quite such a fool (begging your pardon) as to anger our master or make James ashamed of me.
passages.vernacular: 「無疑你會,」梅利萊格斯講;「不過我可冇咁傻(恕我直言)去惹怒我哋嘅主人或讓詹姆斯為我感到羞恥。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「無疑你會,」梅利萊格斯說;「可是我可沒有那麼傻(恕我直言)去惹怒我們的主人或讓詹姆斯為我感到羞恥。

passages.original: Besides, those children are under my charge when they are riding; I tell you they are intrusted to me.
passages.vernacular: 再講,嗰啲細路騎我嘅時候係由我負責嘅;我告訴你,佢哋係託付畀我嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 再說,那些孩子騎我的時候是由我負責的;我告訴你,他們是託付給我的。

passages.original: Why, only the other day I heard our master say to Mrs. Blomefield, 'My dear madam, you need not be anxious about the children; my old Merrylegs will take as much care of them as you or I could; I assure you I would not sell that pony for any money, he is so perfectly good-tempered and trustworthy;' and do you think I am such an ungrateful brute as to forget all the kind treatment I have had here for five years, and all the trust they place in me, and turn vicious because a couple of ignorant boys used me badly?
passages.vernacular: 嗨,就喺前幾天我聽到我哋主人對布洛姆菲爾德太太講:『親愛嘅夫人,您唔使為細路哋擔心;我嘅老梅利萊格斯會像您或我一樣細心照顧佢哋;我向您保證,我唔會為任何錢賣掉嗰匹小馬,佢係咁好脾氣、可靠;』你覺得我會係咁忘恩負義嘅畜生,忘咗我喺呢度五年嚟受到嘅所有善待,同佢哋對我嘅所有信任,而因為兩個無知嘅男孩對我不好就變得凶狠嗎?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 嗨,就在前幾天我聽到我們主人對布洛姆菲爾德太太說:『親愛的夫人,您不必為孩子們擔心;我的老梅利萊格斯會像您或我一樣細心照顧他們;我向您保證,我不會為任何錢賣掉那匹小馬,他是那麼好脾氣、可靠;』你覺得我會是那麼忘恩負義的畜生,忘了我在這裡五年來受到的所有善待,和他們對我的所有信任,而因為兩個無知的男孩對我不好就變得凶狠嗎?

passages.original: No, no! you never had a good place where they were kind to you, and so you don't know, and I'm sorry for you; but I can tell you good places make good horses.
passages.vernacular: 不,不!你從冇過一個佢哋對你好嘅好地方,所以你不明白,我為你難過;不過我可以告訴你,好地方造就好馬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不,不!你從沒有過一個他們對你好的好地方,所以你不明白,我為你難過;不過我可以告訴你,好地方造就好馬。

passages.original: I wouldn't vex our people for anything; I love them, I do,” said Merrylegs, and he gave a low “ho, ho, ho!” through his nose, as he used to do in the morning when he heard James' footstep at the door.
passages.vernacular: 我唔會為任何事惹我哋嘅人生氣;我愛佢哋,真嘅,」梅利萊格斯講,佢從鼻子裡發出一聲低低嘅「嗬、嗬、嗬!」,像佢早晨聽到詹姆斯嘅腳步聲喺門口時常做嘅嗰樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我不會為任何事惹我們的人生氣;我愛他們,真的,」梅利萊格斯說,他從鼻子裡發出一聲低低的「嗬、嗬、嗬!」,像他早晨聽到詹姆斯的腳步聲在門口時常做的那樣。

passages.original: “Besides,” he went on, “if I took to kicking where should I be?
passages.vernacular: 「再講,」佢接住講,「如果我開始亂踢,我會落到邊度?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「再說,」他接著說,「如果我開始亂踢,我會落到哪裡?

passages.original: Why, sold off in a jiffy, and no character, and I might find myself slaved about under a butcher's boy, or worked to death at some seaside place where no one cared for me, except to find out how fast I could go, or be flogged along in some cart with three or four great men in it going out for a Sunday spree, as I have often seen in the place I lived in before I came here; no,” said he, shaking his head, “I hope I shall never come to that.”
passages.vernacular: 嗨,轉眼就被賣掉,冇好名聲,我可能發現自己喺一個肉鋪夥計手下被當奴隸使,或者喺某個冇人關心我嘅海濱地方被活活累死,佢哋只想知道我能跑多快,或者被抽打住拉一輛裡面坐住三四個大漢、去週日狂歡嘅車,像我嚟呢度之前住嘅地方我常見到嘅嗰樣;不,」佢搖住頭講,「我希望我永遠唔好落到嗰一步。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 嗨,轉眼就被賣掉,沒有好名聲,我可能發現自己在一個肉鋪夥計手下被當奴隸使,或者在某個沒人關心我的海濱地方被活活累死,他們只想知道我能跑多快,或者被抽打著拉一輛裡面坐著三四個大漢、去週日狂歡的車,像我來這裡之前住的地方我常見到的那樣;不,」他搖著頭說,「我希望我永遠不要落到那一步。」

chapters.title: Part I · 10 A Talk in the Orchard 第一部·10 果園裡的談話

passages.original: CH Ginger and I were not of the regular tall carriage horse breed, we had more of the racing blood in us.
passages.vernacular: 金姐同我唔係常規嘅高大馬車馬品種,我哋身上有更多賽馬嘅血統。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 金姐和我不是常規的高大馬車馬品種,我們身上有更多賽馬的血統。

passages.original: We stood about fifteen and a half hands high; we were therefore just as good for riding as we were for driving, and our master used to say that he disliked either horse or man that could do but one thing; and as he did not want to show off in London parks, he preferred a more active and useful kind of horse.
passages.vernacular: 我哋大約十五掌半高;所以我哋騎乘同拉車一樣好,我哋嘅主人常講,佢不鍾意只能做一件事嘅馬或人;而且因為佢唔想喺倫敦公園裡炫耀,佢更鍾意一種更活躍有用嘅馬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們大約十五掌半高;所以我們騎乘和拉車一樣好,我們的主人常說,他不喜歡只能做一件事的馬或人;而且因為他不想在倫敦公園裡炫耀,他更喜歡一種更活躍有用的馬。

passages.original: As for us, our greatest pleasure was when we were saddled for a riding party; the master on Ginger, the mistress on me, and the young ladies on Sir Oliver and Merrylegs.
passages.vernacular: 對我哋來講,最大嘅快樂係我哋被套上鞍子去騎行聚會嘅時候;主人騎金姐,女主人騎我,年輕小姐哋騎奧利弗爵士同梅利萊格斯。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 對我們來說,最大的快樂是我們被套上鞍子去騎行聚會的時候;主人騎金姐,女主人騎我,年輕小姐們騎奧利弗爵士和梅利萊格斯。

passages.original: It was so cheerful to be trotting and cantering all together that it always put us in high spirits.
passages.vernacular: 大家一起小跑同飛奔咁令人開心,總讓我哋精神振奮。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 大家一起小跑和飛奔那麼令人開心,總讓我們精神振奮。

passages.original: I had the best of it, for I always carried the mistress; her weight was little, her voice was sweet, and her hand was so light on the rein that I was guided almost without feeling it.
passages.vernacular: 我係最好嘅,因為我總是載女主人;佢嘅重量輕,佢嘅聲音甜美,佢攞韁繩嘅手咁輕,我幾乎感覺唔到就被引導喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我是最好的,因為我總是載女主人;她的重量輕,她的聲音甜美,她拿韁繩的手那麼輕,我幾乎感覺不到就被引導了。

passages.original: Oh! if people knew what a comfort to horses a light hand is, and how it keeps a good mouth and a good temper, they surely would not chuck, and drag, and pull at the rein as they often do.
passages.vernacular: 哦!如果人哋知道輕柔嘅手對馬係多大嘅安慰,佢點樣保持好嘴巴同好脾氣,佢哋肯定唔會像常做嘅嗰樣猛拽、拖拉、拉扯韁繩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 哦!如果人們知道輕柔的手對馬是多大的安慰,它怎樣保持好嘴巴和好脾氣,他們肯定不會像常做的那樣猛拽、拖拉、拉扯韁繩。

passages.original: Our mouths are so tender that where they have not been spoiled or hardened with bad or ignorant treatment, they feel the slightest movement of the driver's hand, and we know in an instant what is required of us.
passages.vernacular: 我哋嘅嘴巴咁嬌嫩,如果佢哋冇被糟糕或無知嘅對待弄壞或弄硬,就能感覺到趕車人手嘅最輕微嘅動作,我哋即刻就知道要我哋做乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們的嘴巴那麼嬌嫩,如果它們沒有被糟糕或無知的對待弄壞或弄硬,就能感覺到趕車人手的最輕微的動作,我們立刻就知道要我們做什麼。

passages.original: My mouth has never been spoiled, and I believe that was why the mistress preferred me to Ginger, although her paces were certainly quite as good.
passages.vernacular: 我嘅嘴從冇被弄壞,我相信呢個就係女主人鍾意我勝過金姐嘅原因,雖然佢嘅步伐確實一樣好。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我的嘴從沒被弄壞,我相信這就是女主人喜歡我勝過金姐的原因,雖然她的步伐確實一樣好。

passages.original: She used often to envy me, and said it was all the fault of breaking in, and the gag bit in London, that her mouth was not so perfect as mine; and then old Sir Oliver would say, “There, there! don't vex yourself; you have the greatest honor; a mare that can carry a tall man of our master's weight, with all your spring and sprightly action, does not need to hold her head down because she does not carry the lady; we horses must take things as they come, and always be contented and willing so long as we are kindly used.”
passages.vernacular: 佢常常羨慕我,講都係馴服同倫敦嘅口銜嘅錯,佢嘅嘴才冇我嘅咁完美;然後老奧利弗爵士會講:「好喇,好喇!別煩惱;你有最大嘅榮耀;一匹能載像我哋主人嗰樣體重嘅高個子男人、有你嗰樣嘅彈跳同活潑動作嘅母馬,不需要因為佢不載女士而垂頭;我哋馬必須順其自然,只要被善待,就永遠知足同心甘情願。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她常常羨慕我,說都是馴服和倫敦的口銜的錯,她的嘴才沒有我的那麼完美;然後老奧利弗爵士會說:「好了,好了!別煩惱;你有最大的榮耀;一匹能載像我們主人那樣體重的高個子男人、有你那樣的彈跳和活潑動作的母馬,不需要因為她不載女士而垂頭;我們馬必須順其自然,只要被善待,就永遠知足和心甘情願。」

passages.original: I had often wondered how it was that Sir Oliver had such a very short tail; it really was only six or seven inches long, with a tassel of hair hanging from it; and on one of our holidays in the orchard I ventured to ask him by what accident it was that he had lost his tail.
passages.vernacular: 我常納悶點解奧利弗爵士嘅尾巴咁短;佢真嘅只有六七英寸長,垂住一綹毛;喺我哋一次果園嘅假日,我冒昧地問佢係點樣嘅意外使佢失去咗尾巴。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我常納悶為什麼奧利弗爵士的尾巴那麼短;它真的只有六七英寸長,垂著一綹毛;在我們一次果園的假日,我冒昧地問他是怎樣的意外使他失去了尾巴。

passages.original: “Accident!” he snorted with a fierce look, “it was no accident! it was a cruel, shameful, cold-blooded act!
passages.vernacular: 「意外!」佢帶住凶狠嘅神情噴住鼻息講,「嗰唔係意外!嗰個係殘忍、可恥、冷血嘅行為!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「意外!」他帶著凶狠的神情噴著鼻息說,「那不是意外!那是殘忍、可恥、冷血的行為!

passages.original: When I was young I was taken to a place where these cruel things were done; I was tied up, and made fast so that I could not stir, and then they came and cut off my long and beautiful tail, through the flesh and through the bone, and took it away.
passages.vernacular: 我年輕嘅時候,被帶到一個做呢啲殘忍事嘅地方;我被拴起嚟,固定住,動彈唔得,然後佢哋嚟喇,把我又長又美嘅尾巴,穿過肉、穿過骨頭,割咗下嚟,攞走喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我年輕的時候,被帶到一個做這些殘忍事的地方;我被拴起來,固定住,動彈不得,然後他們來了,把我又長又美的尾巴,穿過肉、穿過骨頭,割了下來,拿走了。」

passages.original: “How dreadful!”
passages.vernacular: 「多可怕!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「多可怕!」

passages.original: I exclaimed.
passages.vernacular: 我喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我喊道。

passages.original: “Dreadful, ah! it was dreadful; but it was not only the pain, though that was terrible and lasted a long time; it was not only the indignity of having my best ornament taken from me, though that was bad; but it was this, how could I ever brush the flies off my sides and my hind legs any more?
passages.vernacular: 「可怕,啊!係可怕;但不只係疼痛,雖然嗰好可怕,持續咗好長時間;都不只係我最好嘅裝飾被攞走嘅屈辱,雖然嗰都好糟;而係呢個,我點仲能把蒼蠅從我嘅兩側同後腿上趕走呢?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「可怕,啊!是可怕;但不只是疼痛,雖然那很可怕,持續了很長時間;也不只是我最好的裝飾被拿走的屈辱,雖然那也很糟;而是這個,我怎麼還能把蒼蠅從我的兩側和後腿上趕走呢?

passages.original: You who have tails just whisk the flies off without thinking about it, and you can't tell what a torment it is to have them settle upon you and sting and sting, and have nothing in the world to lash them off with.
passages.vernacular: 你哋有尾巴嘅,不假思索地一甩就把蒼蠅趕走喇,你哋講不出當佢哋落喺你身上蜇咗又蜇、而世上卻冇任何嘢可以把佢哋抽走時,係幾咁折磨。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你們有尾巴的,不假思索地一甩就把蒼蠅趕走了,你們說不出當它們落在你身上蜇了又蜇、而世上卻沒有任何東西可以把它們抽走時,是多麼折磨。

passages.original: I tell you it is a lifelong wrong, and a lifelong loss; but thank heaven, they don't do it now.”
passages.vernacular: 我告訴你,呢個係終身嘅冤屈,終身嘅損失;但感謝上天,佢哋而家不咁做喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我告訴你,這是終身的冤屈,終身的損失;但感謝上天,他們現在不這麼做了。」

passages.original: “What did they do it for then?” said Ginger.
passages.vernacular: 「嗰佢哋嗰時點解咁樣做?」金姐講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那他們那時為什麼這樣做?」金姐說。

passages.original: “For fashion!” said the old horse with a stamp of his foot; “for fashion! if you know what that means; there was not a well-bred young horse in my time that had not his tail docked in that shameful way, just as if the good God that made us did not know what we wanted and what looked best.”
passages.vernacular: 「為了時尚!」老馬跺咗一下腳講;「為了時尚!如果你知道嗰個係乜嘢意思;喺我嗰個時代,冇一匹出身良好嘅年輕馬冇被嗰樣可恥地剪斷尾巴,好像創造我哋嘅好上帝唔知道我哋想要乜嘢、乜嘢睇起嚟最好似嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「為了時尚!」老馬跺了一下腳說;「為了時尚!如果你知道那是什麼意思;在我那個時代,沒有一匹出身良好的年輕馬沒有被那樣可恥地剪斷尾巴,好像創造我們的好上帝不知道我們想要什麼、什麼看起來最好似的。」

passages.original: “I suppose it is fashion that makes them strap our heads up with those horrid bits that I was tortured with in London,” said Ginger.
passages.vernacular: 「我想係時尚讓佢哋用嗰啲我喺倫敦受折磨嘅可怕嚼子把我哋嘅頭勒起嚟,」金姐講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我想是時尚讓他們用那些我在倫敦受折磨的可怕嚼子把我們的頭勒起來,」金姐說。

passages.original: “Of course it is,” said he; “to my mind, fashion is one of the wickedest things in the world.
passages.vernacular: 「當然係,」佢講;「喺我睇來,時尚係世上最邪惡嘅事之一。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「當然是,」他說;「在我看來,時尚是世上最邪惡的事之一。

passages.original: Now look, for instance, at the way they serve dogs, cutting off their tails to make them look plucky, and shearing up their pretty little ears to a point to make them both look sharp, forsooth.
passages.vernacular: 而家睇睇,比如講,佢哋點樣對待狗,剪掉牠哋嘅尾巴使牠哋睇起嚟有膽量,把牠哋漂亮嘅小耳朵剪尖,使佢哋兩個都睇起嚟敏銳,真係嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 現在看看,比如說,他們怎樣對待狗,剪掉牠們的尾巴使牠們看起來有膽量,把牠們漂亮的小耳朵剪尖,使它們兩個都看起來敏銳,真是的。

passages.original: I had a dear friend once, a brown terrier; 'Skye' they called her.
passages.vernacular: 我曾經有個親愛嘅朋友,一隻棕色嘅㹴犬;佢哋叫佢『斯凱』。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我曾經有個親愛的朋友,一隻棕色的㹴犬;他們叫她『斯凱』。

passages.original: She was so fond of me that she never would sleep out of my stall; she made her bed under the manger, and there she had a litter of five as pretty little puppies as need be; none were drowned, for they were a valuable kind, and how pleased she was with them! and when they got their eyes open and crawled about, it was a real pretty sight; but one day the man came and took them all away; I thought he might be afraid I should tread upon them.
passages.vernacular: 佢咁鍾意我,從不瞓喺我嘅馬棚外面;佢把床安喺槽底下,喺嗰度生咗一窩五隻漂亮嘅小狗,唔能夠再漂亮喇;冇一隻被淹死,因為佢哋係珍貴嘅品種,佢幾咁高興啊!當佢哋睜開眼睛爬嚟爬去時,係真正漂亮嘅景象;不過有一天嗰個人嚟把佢哋全帶走喇;我想佢可能怕我會踩到佢哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她那麼喜歡我,從不睡在我的馬棚外面;她把床安在槽底下,在那裡生了一窩五隻漂亮的小狗,不能再漂亮了;沒有一隻被淹死,因為它們是珍貴的品種,她多麼高興啊!當它們睜開眼睛爬來爬去時,是真正漂亮的景象;可是有一天那個人來把它們全帶走了;我想他可能怕我會踩到它們。

passages.original: But it was not so; in the evening poor Skye brought them back again, one by one in her mouth; not the happy little things that they were, but bleeding and crying pitifully; they had all had a piece of their tails cut off, and the soft flap of their pretty little ears was cut quite off.
passages.vernacular: 但唔係嗰樣;傍晚時可憐嘅斯凱把佢哋一隻一隻地叼咗回嚟;唔再係快樂嘅小嘢,而係流住血、可憐地哭泣;佢哋都被剪掉咗一截尾巴,漂亮小耳朵上嘅軟垂耳尖被整個剪掉喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 但不是那樣;傍晚時可憐的斯凱把它們一隻一隻地叼了回來;不再是快樂的小東西,而是流著血、可憐地哭泣;它們都被剪掉了一截尾巴,漂亮小耳朵上的軟垂耳尖被整個剪掉了。

passages.original: How their mother licked them, and how troubled she was, poor thing!
passages.vernacular: 佢哋嘅母親點樣舔佢哋,佢幾咁難過啊,可憐嘅嘢!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 它們的母親怎樣舔它們,她多麼難過啊,可憐的東西!

passages.original: I never forgot it.
passages.vernacular: 我從冇忘記過。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我從沒忘記過。

passages.original: They healed in time, and they forgot the pain, but the nice soft flap, that of course was intended to protect the delicate part of their ears from dust and injury, was gone forever.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋時間長咗傷口癒合,忘記咗痛,但嗰片柔軟嘅耳垂,當然本來係為了保護耳朵嘅嬌嫩部分免受灰塵同傷害嘅,永遠冇喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 它們時間長了傷口癒合,忘記了痛,但那片柔軟的耳垂,當然本來是為了保護耳朵的嬌嫩部分免受灰塵和傷害的,永遠沒有了。

passages.original: Why don't they cut their own children's ears into points to make them look sharp?
passages.vernacular: 佢哋點解不把自己細路嘅耳朵剪尖,好讓佢哋睇起嚟敏銳呢?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們為什麼不把自己孩子的耳朵剪尖,好讓他們看起來敏銳呢?

passages.original: Why don't they cut the end off their noses to make them look plucky?
passages.vernacular: 佢哋點解不把自己嘅鼻尖剪掉,讓佢哋睇起嚟有膽量呢?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們為什麼不把自己的鼻尖剪掉,讓他們看起來有膽量呢?

passages.original: One would be just as sensible as the other.
passages.vernacular: 一個同另一個一樣有道理。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一個和另一個一樣有道理。

passages.original: What right have they to torment and disfigure God's creatures?”
passages.vernacular: 佢哋有乜嘢權利折磨同毀傷上帝嘅創造物?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們有什麼權利折磨和毀傷上帝的創造物?」

passages.original: Sir Oliver, though he was so gentle, was a fiery old fellow, and what he said was all so new to me, and so dreadful, that I found a bitter feeling toward men rise up in my mind that I never had before.
passages.vernacular: 奧利弗爵士雖然咁溫和,卻係個火暴脾氣嘅老傢伙,佢講嘅一切對我來講咁新、咁可怕,我心中升起一種我以前從冇過嘅對人嘅苦澀感情。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 奧利弗爵士雖然那麼溫和,卻是個火暴脾氣的老傢伙,他說的一切對我來說那麼新、那麼可怕,我心中升起一種我以前從沒有過的對人的苦澀感情。

passages.original: Of course Ginger was very much excited; she flung up her head with flashing eyes and distended nostrils, declaring that men were both brutes and blockheads.
passages.vernacular: 當然金姐好激動;佢猛地揚起頭,眼睛閃光,鼻孔張大,宣稱人係畜生,都係笨蛋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然金姐非常激動;她猛地揚起頭,眼睛閃光,鼻孔張大,宣稱人是畜生,也是笨蛋。

passages.original: “Who talks about blockheads?” said Merrylegs, who just came up from the old apple-tree, where he had been rubbing himself against the low branch.
passages.vernacular: 「邊個喺講笨蛋?」梅利萊格斯講,佢剛從老蘋果樹嗰度過嚟,喺嗰度佢靠住低矮嘅樹枝蹭癢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「誰在說笨蛋?」梅利萊格斯說,他剛從老蘋果樹那裡過來,在那裡他靠著低矮的樹枝蹭癢。

passages.original: “Who talks about blockheads?
passages.vernacular: 「邊個喺講笨蛋?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「誰在說笨蛋?

passages.original: I believe that is a bad word.”
passages.vernacular: 我想嗰個係個壞詞。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我想那是個壞詞。」

passages.original: “Bad words were made for bad things,” said Ginger, and she told him what Sir Oliver had said.
passages.vernacular: 「壞詞係為壞事造嘅,」金姐講,佢把奧利弗爵士講嘅告訴咗佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「壞詞是為壞事造的,」金姐說,她把奧利弗爵士說的告訴了他。

passages.original: “It is all true,” said Merrylegs sadly, “and I've seen that about the dogs over and over again where I lived first; but we won't talk about it here.
passages.vernacular: 「呢都係真嘅,」梅利萊格斯悲傷地講,「我喺最初住嘅地方都一次又一次見過狗嘅事;不過我哋喺呢度不談呢個。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這都是真的,」梅利萊格斯悲傷地說,「我在最初住的地方也一次又一次見過狗的事;不過我們在這裡不談這個。

passages.original: You know that master, and John and James are always good to us, and talking against men in such a place as this doesn't seem fair or grateful, and you know there are good masters and good grooms beside ours, though of course ours are the best.”
passages.vernacular: 你知道主人、約翰同詹姆斯對我哋總是好好,喺咁樣一個地方講人壞話似乎既不公平都唔知恩,而且你知道除咗我哋嘅,仲有別嘅好主人同好馬夫,當然我哋嘅係最好嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 你知道主人、約翰和詹姆斯對我們總是很好,在這樣一個地方說人壞話似乎既不公平也不知恩,而且你知道除了我們的,還有別的好主人和好馬夫,當然我們的是最好的。」

passages.original: This wise speech of good little Merrylegs, which we knew was quite true, cooled us all down, especially Sir Oliver, who was dearly fond of his master; and to turn the subject I said, “Can any one tell me the use of blinkers?”
passages.vernacular: 好心嘅小梅利萊格斯呢番明智嘅話,我哋知道完全係真嘅,讓我哋都冷靜下嚟,尤其係好喜愛主人嘅奧利弗爵士;為了轉移話題,我講:「有邊個能告訴我遮眼罩有乜嘢用嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 好心的小梅利萊格斯這番明智的話,我們知道完全是真的,讓我們都冷靜下來,尤其是非常喜愛主人的奧利弗爵士;為了轉移話題,我說:「有誰能告訴我遮眼罩有什麼用嗎?」

passages.original: “No!” said Sir Oliver shortly, “because they are no use.”
passages.vernacular: 「冇!」奧利弗爵士簡短地講,「因為佢哋冇用。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「沒有!」奧利弗爵士簡短地說,「因為它們沒有用。」

passages.original: “They are supposed,” said Justice, the roan cob, in his calm way, “to prevent horses from shying and starting, and getting so frightened as to cause accidents.”
passages.vernacular: 「據講,」花斑矮腳馬賈斯蒂斯用佢平靜嘅方式講,「係為了防止馬驚躲同受驚,嚇得引起事故。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「據說,」花斑矮腳馬賈斯蒂斯用他平靜的方式說,「是為了防止馬驚躲和受驚,嚇得引起事故。」

passages.original: “Then what is the reason they do not put them on riding horses; especially on ladies' horses?” said I.
passages.vernacular: 「嗰點解不畀騎乘馬戴,尤其係女士嘅馬?」我講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那為什麼不給騎乘馬戴,尤其是女士的馬?」我說。

passages.original: “There is no reason at all,” said he quietly, “except the fashion; they say that a horse would be so frightened to see the wheels of his own cart or carriage coming behind him that he would be sure to run away, although of course when he is ridden he sees them all about him if the streets are crowded.
passages.vernacular: 「根本冇理由,」佢平靜地講,「除咗時尚;佢哋講,一匹馬睇到自己拉嘅車或馬車嘅輪子喺後面過嚟,會嚇得肯定逃跑,雖然當然被騎嘅時候,如果街上擁擠,佢睇到佢哋就喺佢周圍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「根本沒有理由,」他平靜地說,「除了時尚;他們說,一匹馬看到自己拉的車或馬車的輪子在後面過來,會嚇得肯定逃跑,雖然當然被騎的時候,如果街上擁擠,他看到它們就在他周圍。

passages.original: I admit they do sometimes come too close to be pleasant, but we don't run away; we are used to it, and understand it, and if we never had blinkers put on we should never want them; we should see what was there, and know what was what, and be much less frightened than by only seeing bits of things that we can't understand.
passages.vernacular: 我承認佢哋有時確實靠得太近,不太愉快,但我哋不逃跑;我哋習慣喇,都理解佢,如果我哋從冇戴過遮眼罩,我哋永遠唔會需要佢哋;我哋會睇到嗰度有乜嘢,知道係點回事,比只睇到我哋不明白嘅嘢嘅片段要少害怕得多。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我承認它們有時確實靠得太近,不太愉快,但我們不逃跑;我們習慣了,也理解它,如果我們從沒戴過遮眼罩,我們永遠不會需要它們;我們會看到那裡有什麼,知道是怎麼回事,比只看到我們不明白的東西的片段要少害怕得多。

passages.original: Of course there may be some nervous horses who have been hurt or frightened when they were young, who may be the better for them; but as I never was nervous, I can't judge.”
passages.vernacular: 當然或者有些神經質嘅馬,年輕時受過傷或驚嚇,戴上遮眼罩可能更好;但因為我從來不神經質,我唔能夠判斷。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然也許有些神經質的馬,年輕時受過傷或驚嚇,戴上遮眼罩可能更好;但因為我從來不神經質,我不能判斷。」

passages.original: “I consider,” said Sir Oliver, “that blinkers are dangerous things in the night; we horses can see much better in the dark than men can, and many an accident would never have happened if horses might have had the full use of their eyes.
passages.vernacular: 「我認為,」奧利弗爵士講,「遮眼罩喺夜裡係危險嘅嘢;我哋馬喺黑暗中比人睇得清楚得多,如果馬能充分使用佢哋嘅眼睛,許多事故就永遠唔會發生。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我認為,」奧利弗爵士說,「遮眼罩在夜裡是危險的東西;我們馬在黑暗中比人看得清楚得多,如果馬能充分使用它們的眼睛,許多事故就永遠不會發生。

passages.original: Some years ago, I remember, there was a hearse with two horses returning one dark night, and just by Farmer Sparrow's house, where the pond is close to the road, the wheels went too near the edge, and the hearse was overturned into the water; both the horses were drowned, and the driver hardly escaped.
passages.vernacular: 多年前,我記得有一輛靈車,帶住兩匹馬,喺一個黑夜裡返回,就喺斯派羅農夫嘅房子旁邊,嗰度池塘靠近路邊,車輪離邊緣太近,靈車翻進咗水裡;兩匹馬都淹死喇,趕車人好唔容易才逃脫。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 多年前,我記得有一輛靈車,帶著兩匹馬,在一個黑夜裡返回,就在斯派羅農夫的房子旁邊,那裡池塘靠近路邊,車輪離邊緣太近,靈車翻進了水裡;兩匹馬都淹死了,趕車人好不容易才逃脫。

passages.original: Of course after this accident a stout white rail was put up that might be easily seen, but if those horses had not been partly blinded, they would of themselves have kept further from the edge, and no accident would have happened.
passages.vernacular: 當然呢次事故之後,豎起咗一道結實嘅白色欄杆,容易睇見,但如果嗰啲馬冇被部分遮住眼睛,佢哋自己就會離邊緣更遠,事故就唔會發生喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然這次事故之後,豎起了一道結實的白色欄杆,容易看見,但如果那些馬沒有被部分遮住眼睛,它們自己就會離邊緣更遠,事故就不會發生了。

passages.original: When our master's carriage was overturned, before you came here, it was said that if the lamp on the left side had not gone out, John would have seen the great hole that the road-makers had left; and so he might, but if old Colin had not had blinkers on he would have seen it, lamp or no lamp, for he was far too knowing an old horse to run into danger.
passages.vernacular: 喺你嚟呢度之前,我哋主人嘅馬車翻咗嘅時候,據講如果左邊嘅燈冇滅,約翰就會睇見修路人留下嘅嗰個大洞;或者係咁樣,但如果老科林冇戴遮眼罩,不管有冇燈,佢都會睇見,因為佢係匹太聰明嘅老馬,唔會跑進危險裡。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在你來這裡之前,我們主人的馬車翻了的時候,據說如果左邊的燈沒有滅,約翰就會看見修路人留下的那個大洞;也許是這樣,但如果老科林沒戴遮眼罩,不管有沒有燈,他都會看見,因為他是匹太聰明的老馬,不會跑進危險裡。

passages.original: As it was, he was very much hurt, the carriage was broken, and how John escaped nobody knew.”
passages.vernacular: 結果,佢傷得好重,馬車壞喇,約翰點逃脫嘅冇人知道。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 結果,他傷得很重,馬車壞了,約翰怎麼逃脫的沒有人知道。」

passages.original: “I should say,” said Ginger, curling her nostril, “that these men, who are so wise, had better give orders that in the future all foals should be born with their eyes set just in the middle of their foreheads, instead of on the side; they always think they can improve upon nature and mend what God has made.”
passages.vernacular: 「我該講,」金姐撇住鼻孔講,「呢啲如此聰明嘅人,最好下令以後所有嘅小馬駒都生下嚟,眼睛長喺額頭正中間,而唔係長喺兩側;佢哋總以為能改進自然,修補上帝造嘅嘢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我該說,」金姐撇著鼻孔說,「這些如此聰明的人,最好下令以後所有的小馬駒都生下來,眼睛長在額頭正中間,而不是長在兩側;他們總以為能改進自然,修補上帝造的東西。」

passages.original: Things were getting rather sore again, when Merrylegs held up his knowing little face and said, “I'll tell you a secret: I believe John does not approve of blinkers; I heard him talking with master about it one day.
passages.vernacular: 事情又變得有點傷感時,梅利萊格斯舉起佢聰明嘅小臉講:「我告訴你哋一個祕密:我相信約翰不贊成遮眼罩;有一天我聽到佢同主人談呢件事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 事情又變得有點傷感時,梅利萊格斯舉起他聰明的小臉說:「我告訴你們一個祕密:我相信約翰不贊成遮眼罩;有一天我聽到他同主人談這件事。

passages.original: The master said that 'if horses had been used to them, it might be dangerous in some cases to leave them off'; and John said he thought it would be a good thing if all colts were broken in without blinkers, as was the case in some foreign countries.
passages.vernacular: 主人講『如果馬習慣咗佢哋,喺某些情況下不戴可能係危險嘅』;約翰講佢認為如果所有小馬駒都不戴遮眼罩被馴服,就像啲外國嗰樣,嗰就好喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 主人說『如果馬習慣了它們,在某些情況下不戴可能是危險的』;約翰說他認為如果所有小馬駒都不戴遮眼罩被馴服,就像一些外國那樣,那就好了。

passages.original: So let us cheer up, and have a run to the other end of the orchard; I believe the wind has blown down some apples, and we might just as well eat them as the slugs.”
passages.vernacular: 所以我哋高興起嚟,跑到果園嘅另一頭去吧;我相信風吹落咗啲蘋果,我哋不妨食咗佢哋,免得被蛞蝓食。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 所以我們高興起來,跑到果園的另一頭去吧;我相信風吹落了一些蘋果,我們不妨吃了它們,免得被蛞蝓吃。」

passages.original: Merrylegs could not be resisted, so we broke off our long conversation, and got up our spirits by munching some very sweet apples which lay scattered on the grass.
passages.vernacular: 梅利萊格斯係無法抗拒嘅,所以我哋結束咗漫長嘅談話,食草地上散落嘅啲好甜嘅蘋果,振奮咗精神。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 梅利萊格斯是無法抗拒的,所以我們結束了漫長的談話,吃草地上散落的一些很甜的蘋果,振奮了精神。

chapters.title: Part I · 11 Plain Speaking 第一部·11 直言不諱

passages.original: CH The longer I lived at Birtwick the more proud and happy I felt at having such a place.
passages.vernacular: 我喺伯特威克住得越久,就越為擁有咁樣一個地方而感到自豪同快樂。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我在伯特威克住得越久,就越為擁有這樣一個地方而感到自豪和快樂。

passages.original: Our master and mistress were respected and beloved by all who knew them; they were good and kind to everybody and everything; not only men and women, but horses and donkeys, dogs and cats, cattle and birds; there was no oppressed or ill-used creature that had not a friend in them, and their servants took the same tone.
passages.vernacular: 我哋嘅主人同女主人受到所有認識佢哋嘅人嘅尊敬同愛戴;佢哋對每個人、每件事物都善良、親切;不僅對男人同女人,都對馬同驢子、狗同貓、牛同鳥;冇邊個受壓迫或受虐待嘅生靈喺佢哋嗰度冇朋友,佢哋嘅僕人都係同樣嘅態度。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們的主人和女主人受到所有認識他們的人的尊敬和愛戴;他們對每個人、每件事物都善良、親切;不僅對男人和女人,也對馬和驢子、狗和貓、牛和鳥;沒有哪個受壓迫或受虐待的生靈在他們那裡沒有朋友,他們的僕人也是同樣的態度。

passages.original: If any of the village children were known to treat any creature cruelly they soon heard about it from the Hall.
passages.vernacular: 如果村裡有細路被知道殘忍地對待任何生物,佢哋好快就會從莊園嗰度聽到。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 如果村裡有孩子被知道殘忍地對待任何生物,他們很快就會從莊園那裡聽到。

passages.original: The squire and Farmer Grey had worked together, as they said, for more than twenty years to get check-reins on the cart-horses done away with, and in our parts you seldom saw them; and sometimes, if mistress met a heavily laden horse with his head strained up she would stop the carriage and get out, and reason with the driver in her sweet serious voice, and try to show him how foolish and cruel it was.
passages.vernacular: 鄉紳同格雷農夫一起努力,正如佢哋講嘅,二十多年喇,要廢除拉車馬嘅止韁繩,喺我哋呢一帶你好少見到;有時,如果女主人遇到一匹負重好大、頭被勒得高高嘅馬,佢會停下馬車下嚟,用佢甜美嚴肅嘅聲音同趕車人講道理,試圖讓佢明白呢個係幾咁愚蠢同殘忍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 鄉紳和格雷農夫一起努力,正如他們說的,二十多年了,要廢除拉車馬的止韁繩,在我們這一帶你很少見到;有時,如果女主人遇到一匹負重很大、頭被勒得高高的馬,她會停下馬車下來,用她甜美嚴肅的聲音同趕車人講道理,試圖讓他明白這是多麼愚蠢和殘忍。

passages.original: I don't think any man could withstand our mistress.
passages.vernacular: 我不認為有邊個男人能抵擋我哋嘅女主人。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我不認為有哪個男人能抵擋我們的女主人。

passages.original: I wish all ladies were like her.
passages.vernacular: 我希望所有女士都像佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我希望所有女士都像她。

passages.original: Our master, too, used to come down very heavy sometimes.
passages.vernacular: 我哋嘅主人有時都會嚴厲地斥責人。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們的主人有時也會嚴厲地斥責人。

passages.original: I remember he was riding me toward home one morning when we saw a powerful man driving toward us in a light pony chaise, with a beautiful little bay pony, with slender legs and a high-bred sensitive head and face.
passages.vernacular: 我記得有一天早晨佢騎住我回家時,我哋睇見一個強壯嘅男人駕住一輛輕便嘅小馬車朝我哋嚟,拉車嘅係一匹漂亮嘅棕色小馬,腿細長,頭同臉高貴敏感。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我記得有一天早晨他騎著我回家時,我們看見一個強壯的男人駕著一輛輕便的小馬車朝我們來,拉車的是一匹漂亮的棕色小馬,腿細長,頭和臉高貴敏感。

passages.original: Just as he came to the park gates the little thing turned toward them; the man, without word or warning, wrenched the creature's head round with such a force and suddenness that he nearly threw it on its haunches.
passages.vernacular: 就喺佢嚟到莊園大門口時,嗰小傢伙轉向咗大門;嗰人冇一句話或警告,猛地把牠嘅頭扭過嚟,力氣咁大、咁突然,幾乎把牠扭得蹲坐到後腿上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 就在他來到莊園大門口時,那小傢伙轉向了大門;那人沒有一句話或警告,猛地把牠的頭扭過來,力氣那麼大、那麼突然,幾乎把牠扭得蹲坐到後腿上。

passages.original: Recovering itself it was going on, when he began to lash it furiously.
passages.vernacular: 牠恢復過嚟繼續走時,佢開始瘋狂地抽打牠。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 牠恢復過來繼續走時,他開始瘋狂地抽打牠。

passages.original: The pony plunged forward, but the strong, heavy hand held the pretty creature back with force almost enough to break its jaw, while the whip still cut into him.
passages.vernacular: 小馬向前猛衝,不過嗰強壯沉重嘅手用幾乎足以弄斷牠下顎嘅力氣把呢漂亮嘅生靈勒住,而鞭子仍然抽喺牠身上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 小馬向前猛衝,可是那強壯沉重的手用幾乎足以弄斷牠下顎的力氣把這漂亮的生靈勒住,而鞭子仍然抽在牠身上。

passages.original: It was a dreadful sight to me, for I knew what fearful pain it gave that delicate little mouth; but master gave me the word, and we were up with him in a second.
passages.vernacular: 嗰對我係可怕嘅景象,因為我知道嗰嬌嫩嘅小嘴有多疼;但主人畀咗我信號,我哋一秒鐘就趕上咗佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那對我是可怕的景象,因為我知道那嬌嫩的小嘴有多疼;但主人給了我信號,我們一秒鐘就趕上了他。

passages.original: “Sawyer,” he cried in a stern voice, “is that pony made of flesh and blood?”
passages.vernacular: 「索耶,」佢用嚴厲嘅聲音喊道,「嗰匹小馬係血肉做嘅嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「索耶,」他用嚴厲的聲音喊道,「那匹小馬是血肉做的嗎?」

passages.original: “Flesh and blood and temper,” he said; “he's too fond of his own will, and that won't suit me.”
passages.vernacular: 「係血肉同脾氣,」佢講;「佢太鍾意自己嘅意志喇,呢可不適合我。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是血肉和脾氣,」他說;「他太喜歡自己的意志了,這可不適合我。」

passages.original: He spoke as if he was in a strong passion.
passages.vernacular: 佢講話像喺強烈嘅怒氣中。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他說話像在強烈的怒氣中。

passages.original: He was a builder who had often been to the park on business.
passages.vernacular: 佢係個建築商,常因事嚟莊園。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他是個建築商,常因事來莊園。

passages.original: “And do you think,” said master sternly, “that treatment like this will make him fond of your will?”
passages.vernacular: 「你認為,」主人嚴厲地講,「咁樣嘅對待會使佢鍾意你嘅意志嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你認為,」主人嚴厲地說,「這樣的對待會使他喜歡你的意志嗎?」

passages.original: “He had no business to make that turn; his road was straight on!” said the man roughly.
passages.vernacular: 「佢冇權利轉嗰個彎;佢嘅路係直行嘅!」嗰人粗暴地講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他沒有權利轉那個彎;他的路是直行的!」那人粗暴地說。

passages.original: “You have often driven that pony up to my place,” said master; “it only shows the creature's memory and intelligence; how did he know that you were not going there again?
passages.vernacular: 「你常駕嗰匹小馬到我家嚟,」主人講;「呢只顯示咗牠嘅記憶力同智力;牠點知道你呢次不去嗰度?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你常駕那匹小馬到我家來,」主人說;「這只顯示了牠的記憶力和智力;牠怎麼知道你這次不去那裡?

passages.original: But that has little to do with it.
passages.vernacular: 不過呢同此無關。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不過這與此無關。

passages.original: I must say, Mr. Sawyer, that a more unmanly, brutal treatment of a little pony it was never my painful lot to witness, and by giving way to such passion you injure your own character as much, nay more, than you injure your horse; and remember, we shall all have to be judged according to our works, whether they be toward man or toward beast.”
passages.vernacular: 我必須講,索耶先生,對一匹小馬呢種更不像男人、更殘暴嘅對待,係我痛苦地目睹過嘅最糟嘅;你屈從於呢種怒氣,對你自己品格嘅傷害,不亞於你對你嘅馬嘅傷害,甚至更甚;記住,我哋都要按我哋嘅行為受審判,無論係對人定係對獸。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我必須說,索耶先生,對一匹小馬這種更不像男人、更殘暴的對待,是我痛苦地目睹過的最糟的;你屈從於這種怒氣,對你自己品格的傷害,不亞於你對你的馬的傷害,甚至更甚;記住,我們都要按我們的行為受審判,無論是對人還是對獸。」

passages.original: Master rode me home slowly, and I could tell by his voice how the thing had grieved him.
passages.vernacular: 主人慢慢騎我回家,我能從佢嘅聲音中聽出,呢件事讓佢幾咁難過。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 主人慢慢騎我回家,我能從他的聲音中聽出,這件事讓他多麼難過。

passages.original: He was just as free to speak to gentlemen of his own rank as to those below him; for another day, when we were out, we met a Captain Langley, a friend of our master's; he was driving a splendid pair of grays in a kind of break.
passages.vernacular: 佢對同階層嘅紳士同對地位低於佢嘅人一樣直言;因為另一天我哋出去時,遇到一位朗格利上尉,係我哋主人嘅朋友;佢駕住一輛華麗嘅灰馬雙駕馬車。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他對同階層的紳士同對地位低於他的人一樣直言;因為另一天我們出去時,遇到一位朗格利上尉,是我們主人的朋友;他駕著一輛華麗的灰馬雙駕馬車。

passages.original: After a little conversation the captain said:
passages.vernacular: 稍微交談之後,上尉講:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 稍微交談之後,上尉說:

passages.original: “What do you think of my new team, Mr. Douglas?
passages.vernacular: 「道格拉斯先生,您覺得我嘅新馬隊點樣?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「道格拉斯先生,您覺得我的新馬隊怎麼樣?

passages.original: You know, you are the judge of horses in these parts, and I should like your opinion.”
passages.vernacular: 您知道,您係呢一帶馬嘅行家,我想聽聽您嘅意見。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 您知道,您是這一帶馬的行家,我想聽聽您的意見。」

passages.original: The master backed me a little, so as to get a good view of them.
passages.vernacular: 主人讓我稍微後退咗啲,以便好好地睇佢哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 主人讓我稍微後退了一點,以便好好地看它們。

passages.original: “They are an uncommonly handsome pair,” he said, “and if they are as good as they look I am sure you need not wish for anything better; but I see you still hold that pet scheme of yours for worrying your horses and lessening their power.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢哋係非同尋常嘅漂亮嘅一對,」佢講,「如果佢哋同睇起嚟一樣好,我確信您不需要期望更好嘅喇;不過我睇您仍然堅持您嗰個折磨馬、減弱佢哋力量嘅寶貝方案。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「它們是非同尋常的漂亮的一對,」他說,「如果它們和看起來一樣好,我確信您不需要期望更好的了;不過我看您仍然堅持您那個折磨馬、減弱它們力量的寶貝方案。」

passages.original: “What do you mean,” said the other, “the check-reins?
passages.vernacular: 「您指乜嘢,」另一個講,「止韁繩嗎?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「您指什麼,」另一個說,「止韁繩嗎?

passages.original: Oh, ah!
passages.vernacular: 哦,啊!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 哦,啊!

passages.original: I know that's a hobby of yours; well, the fact is, I like to see my horses hold their heads up.”
passages.vernacular: 我知道嗰個係您嘅嗜好;好吧,事實係,我鍾意睇我嘅馬昂住頭。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我知道那是您的嗜好;好吧,事實是,我喜歡看我的馬昂著頭。」

passages.original: “So do I,” said master, “as well as any man, but I don't like to see them held up; that takes all the shine out of it.
passages.vernacular: 「我都一樣,」主人講,「同任何人一樣,但我不鍾意睇佢哋被勒住昂頭;嗰把所有嘅光彩都奪走喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我也一樣,」主人說,「和任何人一樣,但我不喜歡看它們被勒著昂頭;那把所有的光彩都奪走了。

passages.original: Now, you are a military man, Langley, and no doubt like to see your regiment look well on parade, 'heads up', and all that; but you would not take much credit for your drill if all your men had their heads tied to a backboard!
passages.vernacular: 而家,您係軍人,朗格利,無疑鍾意睇您嘅團喺閱兵時睇起嚟好好,『昂首挺胸』之類嘅;但如果您所有嘅人嘅頭都被綁喺一塊背板上,您就唔會為您嘅操練感到多少驕傲喇!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 現在,您是軍人,朗格利,無疑喜歡看您的團在閱兵時看起來很好,『昂首挺胸』之類的;但如果您所有的人的頭都被綁在一塊背板上,您就不會為您的操練感到多少驕傲了!

passages.original: It might not be much harm on parade, except to worry and fatigue them; but how would it be in a bayonet charge against the enemy, when they want the free use of every muscle, and all their strength thrown forward?
passages.vernacular: 喺閱兵時,呢或者除咗讓佢哋煩惱疲勞之外,害處不大;不過喺對敵人嘅刺刀衝鋒中會點樣,嗰時佢哋需要充分運用每一塊肌肉,把全部力量向前傾注?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在閱兵時,這也許除了讓他們煩惱疲勞之外,害處不大;可是在對敵人的刺刀衝鋒中會怎樣,那時他們需要充分運用每一塊肌肉,把全部力量向前傾注?

passages.original: I would not give much for their chance of victory.
passages.vernacular: 我唔會睇好佢哋獲勝嘅機會。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我不會看好他們獲勝的機會。

passages.original: And it is just the same with horses: you fret and worry their tempers, and decrease their power; you will not let them throw their weight against their work, and so they have to do too much with their joints and muscles, and of course it wears them up faster.
passages.vernacular: 馬都係完全一樣:您讓佢哋煩惱,使佢哋脾氣暴躁,減弱佢哋嘅力量;您不讓佢哋把重量壓向佢哋嘅工作,所以佢哋唔得不更多地用關節同肌肉,當然呢使佢哋更快地磨損。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 馬也是完全一樣:您讓它們煩惱,使它們脾氣暴躁,減弱它們的力量;您不讓它們把重量壓向它們的工作,所以它們不得不更多地用關節和肌肉,當然這使它們更快地磨損。

passages.original: You may depend upon it, horses were intended to have their heads free, as free as men's are; and if we could act a little more according to common sense, and a good deal less according to fashion, we should find many things work easier; besides, you know as well as I that if a horse makes a false step, he has much less chance of recovering himself if his head and neck are fastened back.
passages.vernacular: 您可以相信,馬生來係要讓頭自由嘅,像人嘅頭一樣自由;如果我哋多按常識、少按時尚行事啲,我哋會發現許多事情更容易做;而且,您同我一樣知道,如果一匹馬失足,頭同脖子被向後勒住,佢恢復嘅機會要小得多。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 您可以相信,馬生來是要讓頭自由的,像人的頭一樣自由;如果我們多按常識、少按時尚行事一些,我們會發現許多事情更容易做;而且,您和我一樣知道,如果一匹馬失足,頭和脖子被向後勒住,它恢復的機會要小得多。

passages.original: And now,” said the master, laughing, “I have given my hobby a good trot out, can't you make up your mind to mount him, too, captain?
passages.vernacular: 而家,」主人笑住講,「我已經讓我嘅嗜好好好跑咗一圈,您就唔能夠下決心都騎上佢嗎,上尉?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 現在,」主人笑著說,「我已經讓我的嗜好好好跑了一圈,您就不能下決心也騎上它嗎,上尉?

passages.original: Your example would go a long way.”
passages.vernacular: 您嘅榜樣會有好大嘅作用。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 您的榜樣會有很大的作用。」

passages.original: “I believe you are right in theory,” said the other, “and that's rather a hard hit about the soldiers; but--well--I'll think about it,” and so they parted.
passages.vernacular: 「我相信您喺理論上係對嘅,」另一個講,「而且您對士兵嘅講法相當有力;不過——好吧——我會考慮嘅,」於是佢哋分手喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我相信您在理論上是對的,」另一個說,「而且您對士兵的說法相當有力;不過——好吧——我會考慮的,」於是他們分手了。

chapters.title: Part I · 12 A Stormy Day 第一部·12 暴風雨的一天

passages.original: CH One day late in the autumn my master had a long journey to go on business.
passages.vernacular: 晚秋嘅一天,我嘅主人有一趟因事出嘅遠門。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 晚秋的一天,我的主人有一趟因事出的遠門。

passages.original: I was put into the dog-cart, and John went with his master.
passages.vernacular: 我被套進狗車,約翰同佢嘅主人一起去。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我被套進狗車,約翰同他的主人一起去。

passages.original: I always liked to go in the dog-cart, it was so light and the high wheels ran along so pleasantly.
passages.vernacular: 我總鍾意拉狗車,佢咁輕,高輪子跑得咁愉快。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我總喜歡拉狗車,它那麼輕,高輪子跑得那麼愉快。

passages.original: There had been a great deal of rain, and now the wind was very high and blew the dry leaves across the road in a shower.
passages.vernacular: 下咗好多雨,而家風好大,把乾樹葉像陣雨般吹過路面。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 下了很多雨,現在風很大,把乾樹葉像陣雨般吹過路面。

passages.original: We went along merrily till we came to the toll-bar and the low wooden bridge.
passages.vernacular: 我哋歡快地一路走,直到來到收費柵欄同低矮嘅木橋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們歡快地一路走,直到來到收費柵欄和低矮的木橋。

passages.original: The river banks were rather high, and the bridge, instead of rising, went across just level, so that in the middle, if the river was full, the water would be nearly up to the woodwork and planks; but as there were good substantial rails on each side, people did not mind it.
passages.vernacular: 河岸相當高,橋冇向上弓起,而係平平地橫過去,所以喺中間,如果河水漲滿,水幾乎能到木欄杆同木板嘅高度;但因為兩邊有結實嘅欄杆,人哋並不在意。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 河岸相當高,橋沒有向上弓起,而是平平地橫過去,所以在中間,如果河水漲滿,水幾乎能到木欄杆和木板的高度;但因為兩邊有結實的欄杆,人們並不在意。

passages.original: The man at the gate said the river was rising fast, and he feared it would be a bad night.
passages.vernacular: 柵門嘅人講河水漲得好快,佢擔心今晚會好糟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柵門的人說河水漲得很快,他擔心今晚會很糟。

passages.original: Many of the meadows were under water, and in one low part of the road the water was halfway up to my knees; the bottom was good, and master drove gently, so it was no matter.
passages.vernacular: 許多草地都被水淹喇,喺路嘅一處低窪地方,水漲到我膝蓋嘅一半;路底好好,主人慢慢地駕車,所以冇關係。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 許多草地都被水淹了,在路的一處低窪地方,水漲到我膝蓋的一半;路底很好,主人慢慢地駕車,所以沒關係。

passages.original: When we got to the town of course I had a good bait, but as the master's business engaged him a long time we did not start for home till rather late in the afternoon.
passages.vernacular: 我哋到咗城裡,我當然好好食咗一頓,不過因為主人嘅事務耽擱咗好長時間,我哋直到下午相當晚才動身回家。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們到了城裡,我當然好好吃了一頓,可是因為主人的事務耽擱了很長時間,我們直到下午相當晚才動身回家。

passages.original: The wind was then much higher, and I heard the master say to John that he had never been out in such a storm; and so I thought, as we went along the skirts of a wood, where the great branches were swaying about like twigs, and the rushing sound was terrible.
passages.vernacular: 嗰時風已經大得多,我聽見主人對約翰講,佢從冇喺咁樣嘅暴風中出過門;我都咁想,我哋沿住一片樹林邊緣走,嗰度大樹枝像細枝一樣搖擺,呼嘯聲好可怕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那時風已經大得多,我聽見主人對約翰說,他從沒在這樣的暴風中出過門;我也這麼想,我們沿著一片樹林邊緣走,那裡大樹枝像細枝一樣搖擺,呼嘯聲很可怕。

passages.original: “I wish we were well out of this wood,” said my master.
passages.vernacular: 「我真希望我哋能順利走出呢片樹林,」我嘅主人講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我真希望我們能順利走出這片樹林,」我的主人說。

passages.original: “Yes, sir,” said John, “it would be rather awkward if one of these branches came down upon us.”
passages.vernacular: 「係,先生,」約翰講,「如果呢啲樹枝中嘅一根掉下嚟砸喺我哋身上,嗰就相當尷尬喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是,先生,」約翰說,「如果這些樹枝中的一根掉下來砸在我們身上,那就相當尷尬了。」

passages.original: The words were scarcely out of his mouth when there was a groan, and a crack, and a splitting sound, and tearing, crashing down among the other trees came an oak, torn up by the roots, and it fell right across the road just before us.
passages.vernacular: 佢嘅話剛出口,就傳嚟一聲呻吟、一聲爆裂、一聲劈開嘅響聲,一棵橡樹連根拔起,撕裂住、轟然倒喺其他樹中間,正好橫倒喺我哋面前嘅路上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他的話剛出口,就傳來一聲呻吟、一聲爆裂、一聲劈開的響聲,一棵橡樹連根拔起,撕裂著、轟然倒在其他樹中間,正好橫倒在我們面前的路上。

passages.original: I will never say I was not frightened, for I was.
passages.vernacular: 我決不講我不害怕,因為我確實害怕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我決不說我不害怕,因為我確實害怕。

passages.original: I stopped still, and I believe I trembled; of course I did not turn round or run away; I was not brought up to that.
passages.vernacular: 我站住不動,我相信我發抖喇;當然我冇轉身或逃跑;我唔係被咁樣教養大嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我站住不動,我相信我發抖了;當然我沒有轉身或逃跑;我不是被這樣教養大的。

passages.original: John jumped out and was in a moment at my head.
passages.vernacular: 約翰跳下嚟,轉眼就到咗我嘅頭旁。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 約翰跳下來,轉眼就到了我的頭旁。

passages.original: “That was a very near touch,” said my master.
passages.vernacular: 「嗰真係千鈞一髮,」我嘅主人講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那真是千鈞一髮,」我的主人說。

passages.original: “What's to be done now?”
passages.vernacular: 「而家該點算?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「現在該怎麼辦?」

passages.original: “Well, sir, we can't drive over that tree, nor yet get round it; there will be nothing for it, but to go back to the four crossways, and that will be a good six miles before we get round to the wooden bridge again; it will make us late, but the horse is fresh.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,先生,我哋唔能夠從嗰棵樹上駛過去,都繞不過去;冇別嘅辦法,只有退回到四岔路口,然後足足六英里才能繞回木橋;呢會讓我哋晚些,但馬仲精神。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,先生,我們不能從那棵樹上駛過去,也繞不過去;沒有別的辦法,只有退回到四岔路口,然後足足六英里才能繞回木橋;這會讓我們晚些,但馬還精神。」

passages.original: So back we went and round by the crossroads, but by the time we got to the bridge it was very nearly dark; we could just see that the water was over the middle of it; but as that happened sometimes when the floods were out, master did not stop.
passages.vernacular: 於是我哋退咗回去,繞過岔路口,我哋到達橋邊時,天幾乎黑喇;我哋只能睇出水喺橋中間之上;但因為洪水氾濫時有時會咁樣,主人冇停下。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是我們退了回去,繞過岔路口,我們到達橋邊時,天幾乎黑了;我們只能看出水在橋中間之上;但因為洪水氾濫時有時會這樣,主人沒有停下。

passages.original: We were going along at a good pace, but the moment my feet touched the first part of the bridge I felt sure there was something wrong.
passages.vernacular: 我哋以不錯嘅步伐前進,但我嘅蹄子一碰到橋嘅第一部分,我就肯定有乜嘢不對勁。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們以不錯的步伐前進,但我的蹄子一碰到橋的第一部分,我就肯定有什麼不對勁。

passages.original: I dare not go forward, and I made a dead stop.
passages.vernacular: 我唔敢向前,我完全停住喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我不敢向前,我完全停住了。

passages.original: “Go on, Beauty,” said my master, and he gave me a touch with the whip, but I dare not stir; he gave me a sharp cut; I jumped, but I dare not go forward.
passages.vernacular: 「走,神駒,」我嘅主人講,佢用鞭子碰咗我一下,可我唔敢動;佢狠狠抽咗我一下;我跳咗起嚟,可我唔敢向前。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「走,神駒,」我的主人說,他用鞭子碰了我一下,可我不敢動;他狠狠抽了我一下;我跳了起來,可我不敢向前。

passages.original: “There's something wrong, sir,” said John, and he sprang out of the dog-cart and came to my head and looked all about.
passages.vernacular: 「有乜嘢不對,先生,」約翰講,佢從狗車上跳下嚟,走到我頭旁,四處睇咗睇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「有什麼不對,先生,」約翰說,他從狗車上跳下來,走到我頭旁,四處看了看。

passages.original: He tried to lead me forward.
passages.vernacular: 佢試住牽我向前。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他試著牽我向前。

passages.original: “Come on, Beauty, what's the matter?”
passages.vernacular: 「嚟,神駒,點喇?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「來,神駒,怎麼了?」

passages.original: Of course I could not tell him, but I knew very well that the bridge was not safe.
passages.vernacular: 當然我唔能夠告訴佢,可我好清楚橋係不安全嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然我不能告訴他,可我很清楚橋是不安全的。

passages.original: Just then the man at the toll-gate on the other side ran out of the house, tossing a torch about like one mad.
passages.vernacular: 就喺呢陣,對面收費柵門嘅人從屋裡跑出嚟,像瘋子一樣揮舞住火把。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 就在這時,對面收費柵門的人從屋裡跑出來,像瘋子一樣揮舞著火把。

passages.original: “Hoy, hoy, hoy! halloo! stop!” he cried.
passages.vernacular: 「嗨、嗨、嗨!喂!停下!」佢喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗨、嗨、嗨!喂!停下!」他喊道。

passages.original: “What's the matter?” shouted my master.
passages.vernacular: 「點喇?」我嘅主人喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「怎麼了?」我的主人喊道。

passages.original: “The bridge is broken in the middle, and part of it is carried away; if you come on you'll be into the river.”
passages.vernacular: 「橋從中間斷喇,一部分被沖走喇;如果你哋過嚟,就會掉進河裡。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「橋從中間斷了,一部分被沖走了;如果你們過來,就會掉進河裡。」

passages.original: “Thank God!” said my master.
passages.vernacular: 「感謝上帝!」我嘅主人講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「感謝上帝!」我的主人說。

passages.original: “You Beauty!” said John, and took the bridle and gently turned me round to the right-hand road by the river side.
passages.vernacular: 「你呢神駒!」約翰講,佢拉起轡頭,輕輕地把我轉向右邊河邊嘅路。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你這神駒!」約翰說,他拉起轡頭,輕輕地把我轉向右邊河邊的路。

passages.original: The sun had set some time; the wind seemed to have lulled off after that furious blast which tore up the tree.
passages.vernacular: 太陽已經落山好一會兒喇;嗰陣撕倒樹嘅猛烈狂風之後,風似乎平息喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 太陽已經落山好一會兒了;那陣撕倒樹的猛烈狂風之後,風似乎平息了。

passages.original: It grew darker and darker, stiller and stiller.
passages.vernacular: 天越嚟越黑,越嚟越靜。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 天越來越黑,越來越靜。

passages.original: I trotted quietly along, the wheels hardly making a sound on the soft road.
passages.vernacular: 我安靜地小跑住,車輪喺鬆軟嘅路上幾乎冇發出聲音。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我安靜地小跑著,車輪在鬆軟的路上幾乎沒發出聲音。

passages.original: For a good while neither master nor John spoke, and then master began in a serious voice.
passages.vernacular: 好長一段時間主人和約翰都冇講話,然後主人用嚴肅嘅聲音開始喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 很長一段時間主人和約翰都沒說話,然後主人用嚴肅的聲音開始了。

passages.original: I could not understand much of what they said, but I found they thought, if I had gone on as the master wanted me, most likely the bridge would have given way under us, and horse, chaise, master, and man would have fallen into the river; and as the current was flowing very strongly, and there was no light and no help at hand, it was more than likely we should all have been drowned.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋講嘅我不太能聽懂,但我發現佢哋認為,如果我按主人要我嘅嗰樣繼續走,橋好可能會喺我哋身下塌掉,馬、馬車、主人同人都會掉進河裡;而且因為水流好急,又冇光,附近都冇人幫忙,我哋好可能都會被淹死。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們說的我不太能聽懂,但我發現他們認為,如果我按主人要我的那樣繼續走,橋很可能會在我們身下塌掉,馬、馬車、主人和人都會掉進河裡;而且因為水流很急,又沒有光,附近也沒有人幫忙,我們很可能都會被淹死。

passages.original: Master said, God had given men reason, by which they could find out things for themselves; but he had given animals knowledge which did not depend on reason, and which was much more prompt and perfect in its way, and by which they had often saved the lives of men.
passages.vernacular: 主人講,上帝畀咗人理性,佢哋憑理性能自己發現事物;但祂畀咗動物不依賴理性嘅知識,佢喺自己嘅方式上快得多、完美得多,動物常憑佢救咗人嘅命。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 主人說,上帝給了人理性,他們憑理性能自己發現事物;但祂給了動物不依賴理性的知識,它在自己的方式上快得多、完美得多,動物常憑它救了人的命。

passages.original: John had many stories to tell of dogs and horses, and the wonderful things they had done; he thought people did not value their animals half enough nor make friends of them as they ought to do.
passages.vernacular: 約翰有許多關於狗同馬嘅故事要講,講佢哋做嘅奇妙嘅事;佢認為人哋對動物嘅重視仲唔到一半,都冇像佢哋應該嘅嗰樣同佢哋交朋友。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 約翰有許多關於狗和馬的故事要講,講它們做的奇妙的事;他認為人們對動物的重視還不到一半,也沒有像他們應該的那樣與它們交朋友。

passages.original: I am sure he makes friends of them if ever a man did.
passages.vernacular: 我確信,如果有邊個人同佢哋交朋友,佢就係。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我確信,如果有哪個人同它們交朋友,他就是。

passages.original: At last we came to the park gates and found the gardener looking out for us.
passages.vernacular: 終於我哋到咗莊園大門口,發現園丁喺等我哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 終於我們到了莊園大門口,發現園丁在等我們。

passages.original: He said that mistress had been in a dreadful way ever since dark, fearing some accident had happened, and that she had sent James off on Justice, the roan cob, toward the wooden bridge to make inquiry after us.
passages.vernacular: 佢講女主人天黑以來一直焦急萬分,擔心出咗乜嘢事故,佢派詹姆斯騎花斑矮腳馬賈斯蒂斯往木橋嗰邊去打聽我哋嘅消息。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他說女主人天黑以來一直焦急萬分,擔心出了什麼事故,她派詹姆斯騎花斑矮腳馬賈斯蒂斯往木橋那邊去打聽我們的消息。

passages.original: We saw a light at the hall-door and at the upper windows, and as we came up mistress ran out, saying, “Are you really safe, my dear?
passages.vernacular: 我哋睇到大廳門口同樓上窗口有燈光,我哋走近時,女主人跑出嚟,講:「你哋真嘅平安嗎,親愛嘅?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們看到大廳門口和樓上窗口有燈光,我們走近時,女主人跑出來,說:「你們真的平安嗎,親愛的?

passages.original: Oh!
passages.vernacular: 哦!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 哦!

passages.original: I have been so anxious, fancying all sorts of things.
passages.vernacular: 我一直咁焦急,想像各種事情。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我一直那麼焦急,想像各種事情。

passages.original: Have you had no accident?”
passages.vernacular: 冇出乜嘢事故吧?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 沒出什麼事故吧?」

passages.original: “No, my dear; but if your Black Beauty had not been wiser than we were we should all have been carried down the river at the wooden bridge.”
passages.vernacular: 「冇,親愛嘅;但如果你嘅黑神駒不比我哋聰明,我哋都會喺木橋被沖進河裡喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「沒有,親愛的;但如果你的黑神駒不比我們聰明,我們都會在木橋被沖進河裡了。」

passages.original: I heard no more, as they went into the house, and John took me to the stable.
passages.vernacular: 我冇再聽到乜嘢,因為佢哋進咗屋,約翰把我帶到咗馬廄。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我沒再聽到什麼,因為他們進了屋,約翰把我帶到了馬廄。

passages.original: Oh, what a good supper he gave me that night, a good bran mash and some crushed beans with my oats, and such a thick bed of straw! and I was glad of it, for I was tired.
passages.vernacular: 哦,嗰天晚上佢畀咗我多好嘅晚餐啊,一份好嘅麩皮糊同啲碾碎嘅豆子配上我嘅燕麥,仲有咁厚嘅一床稻草!我好高興,因為我累喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 哦,那天晚上他給了我多好的晚餐啊,一份好的麩皮糊和一些碾碎的豆子配上我的燕麥,還有那麼厚的一床稻草!我很高興,因為我累了。

chapters.title: Part I · 13 The Devil's Trade Mark 第一部·13 魔鬼的商標

passages.original: CH One day when John and I had been out on some business of our master's, and were returning gently on a long, straight road, at some distance we saw a boy trying to leap a pony over a gate; the pony would not take the leap, and the boy cut him with the whip, but he only turned off on one side.
passages.vernacular: 有一天,約翰同我為主人辦完事,正沿住一條長長嘅直路輕輕往回走,遠處我哋睇見一個男孩試圖讓一匹小馬跳過一道柵門;小馬唔肯跳,男孩用鞭子抽佢,但佢只係轉到一邊。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 有一天,約翰和我為主人辦完事,正沿著一條長長的直路輕輕往回走,遠處我們看見一個男孩試圖讓一匹小馬跳過一道柵門;小馬不肯跳,男孩用鞭子抽它,但它只是轉到一邊。

passages.original: He whipped him again, but the pony turned off on the other side.
passages.vernacular: 佢又抽佢,但小馬又轉到另一邊。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他又抽它,但小馬又轉到另一邊。

passages.original: Then the boy got off and gave him a hard thrashing, and knocked him about the head; then he got up again and tried to make him leap the gate, kicking him all the time shamefully, but still the pony refused.
passages.vernacular: 然後男孩下嚟狠狠揍咗佢一頓,打佢嘅頭;然後佢又爬上去,試圖讓佢跳過柵門,一直無恥地踢佢,可小馬仍然拒絕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後男孩下來狠狠揍了它一頓,打它的頭;然後他又爬上去,試圖讓它跳過柵門,一直無恥地踢它,可小馬仍然拒絕。

passages.original: When we were nearly at the spot the pony put down his head and threw up his heels, and sent the boy neatly over into a broad quickset hedge, and with the rein dangling from his head he set off home at a full gallop.
passages.vernacular: 我哋快到嗰地方時,小馬低下頭,尥起後蹄,把男孩乾淨利落地甩進咗一道寬寬嘅山楂樹籬,拖住韁繩從頭上垂下嚟,全速飛奔回家去喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我們快到那地方時,小馬低下頭,尥起後蹄,把男孩乾淨利落地甩進了一道寬寬的山楂樹籬,拖著韁繩從頭上垂下來,全速飛奔回家去了。

passages.original: John laughed out quite loud.
passages.vernacular: 約翰放聲大笑。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 約翰放聲大笑。

passages.original: “Served him right,” he said.
passages.vernacular: 「活該,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「活該,」他說。

passages.original: “Oh, oh, oh!” cried the boy as he struggled about among the thorns; “I say, come and help me out.”
passages.vernacular: 「哦,哦,哦!」男孩喺荊棘中掙扎住喊;「我講,嚟幫我出去。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦,哦,哦!」男孩在荊棘中掙扎著喊;「我說,來幫我出去。」

passages.original: “Thank ye,” said John, “I think you are quite in the right place, and maybe a little scratching will teach you not to leap a pony over a gate that is too high for him,” and so with that John rode off.
passages.vernacular: 「謝謝你,」約翰講,「我想你就喺你該喺嘅地方,或者被扎幾下會教你,唔好畀小馬跳一道對佢太高嘅柵門,」講完約翰騎馬走喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「謝謝你,」約翰說,「我想你就在你該在的地方,也許被扎幾下會教你,別讓小馬跳一道對它太高的柵門,」說完約翰騎馬走了。

passages.original: “It may be,” said he to himself, “that young fellow is a liar as well as a cruel one; we'll just go home by Farmer Bushby's, Beauty, and then if anybody wants to know you and I can tell 'em, ye see.”
passages.vernacular: 「或者,」佢自言自語地講,「嗰小夥子既殘忍又講謊;我哋就從布什比農夫嗰度回家吧,神駒,咁樣如果有人想知道,你同我就可以告訴佢哋喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「也許,」他自言自語地說,「那小夥子既殘忍又說謊;我們就從布什比農夫那裡回家吧,神駒,這樣如果有人想知道,你和我就可以告訴他們了。」

passages.original: So we turned off to the right, and soon came up to the stack-yard, and within sight of the house.
passages.vernacular: 於是我哋向右轉,好快嚟到咗麥垛場,睇得見房子。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是我們向右轉,很快來到了麥垛場,看得見房子。

passages.original: The farmer was hurrying out into the road, and his wife was standing at the gate, looking very frightened.
passages.vernacular: 農夫匆忙跑到路上,佢嘅妻子站喺門口,睇起嚟好害怕。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 農夫匆忙跑到路上,他的妻子站在門口,看起來非常害怕。

passages.original: “Have you seen my boy?” said Mr. Bushby as we came up; “he went out an hour ago on my black pony, and the creature is just come back without a rider.”
passages.vernacular: 「你睇見我兒子咗嗎?」布什比先生喺我哋走近時講;「佢一個小時前騎我嘅黑小馬出去嘅,嗰牲口剛回嚟,冇騎手。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你看見我兒子了嗎?」布什比先生在我們走近時說;「他一個小時前騎我的黑小馬出去的,那牲口剛回來,沒有騎手。」

passages.original: “I should think, sir,” said John, “he had better be without a rider, unless he can be ridden properly.”
passages.vernacular: 「我認為,先生,」約翰講,「佢最好冇騎手,除非佢能正確地騎。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我認為,先生,」約翰說,「他最好沒有騎手,除非他能正確地騎。」

passages.original: “What do you mean?” said the farmer.
passages.vernacular: 「你乜嘢意思?」農夫講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你什麼意思?」農夫說。

passages.original: “Well, sir, I saw your son whipping, and kicking, and knocking that good little pony about shamefully because he would not leap a gate that was too high for him.
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,先生,我睇見您兒子抽打、踢同毆打嗰匹好小馬,可恥地,因為佢唔肯跳一道對佢太高嘅柵門。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,先生,我看見您兒子抽打、踢和毆打那匹好小馬,可恥地,因為它不肯跳一道對它太高的柵門。

passages.original: The pony behaved well, sir, and showed no vice; but at last he just threw up his heels and tipped the young gentleman into the thorn hedge.
passages.vernacular: 小馬表現得好好,先生,冇顯出任何惡習;不過最後佢只係尥起後蹄,把年輕先生摔進咗荊棘樹籬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 小馬表現得很好,先生,沒顯出任何惡習;可是最後它只是尥起後蹄,把年輕先生摔進了荊棘樹籬。

passages.original: He wanted me to help him out, but I hope you will excuse me, sir, I did not feel inclined to do so.
passages.vernacular: 佢要我幫佢出嚟,不過希望您原諒,先生,我唔想咁樣做。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他要我幫他出來,可是希望您原諒,先生,我不想這樣做。

passages.original: There's no bones broken, sir; he'll only get a few scratches.
passages.vernacular: 冇骨頭斷,先生;佢只會有幾處擦傷。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 沒有骨頭斷,先生;他只會有幾處擦傷。

passages.original: I love horses, and it riles me to see them badly used; it is a bad plan to aggravate an animal till he uses his heels; the first time is not always the last.”
passages.vernacular: 我愛馬,睇到佢哋被糟糕地對待讓我惱火;激怒一個動物直到佢尥蹄子係個壞辦法;第一次並不總是最後一次。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我愛馬,看到它們被糟糕地對待讓我惱火;激怒一個動物直到它尥蹄子是個壞辦法;第一次並不總是最後一次。」

passages.original: During this time the mother began to cry, “Oh, my poor Bill, I must go and meet him; he must be hurt.”
passages.vernacular: 呢陣母親開始哭喊:「哦,我可憐嘅比爾,我必須去接佢;佢一定受傷喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這時母親開始哭喊:「哦,我可憐的比爾,我必須去接他;他一定受傷了。」

passages.original: “You had better go into the house, wife,” said the farmer; “Bill wants a lesson about this, and I must see that he gets it; this is not the first time, nor the second, that he has ill-used that pony, and I shall stop it.
passages.vernacular: 「你最好進屋去,老婆,」農夫講;「比爾需要呢方面嘅教訓,我必須確保佢得到;呢唔係第一次,都唔係第二次,佢虐待嗰匹小馬,我要制止佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你最好進屋去,老婆,」農夫說;「比爾需要這方面的教訓,我必須確保他得到;這不是第一次,也不是第二次,他虐待那匹小馬,我要制止它。

passages.original: I am much obliged to you, Manly.
passages.vernacular: 我好感謝你,曼利。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我非常感謝你,曼利。

passages.original: Good-evening.”
passages.vernacular: 晚安。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 晚安。」

passages.original: So we went on, John chuckling all the way home; then he told James about it, who laughed and said, “Serve him right.
passages.vernacular: 於是我哋繼續走,約翰一路上偷笑住回家;然後佢告訴咗詹姆斯,詹姆斯笑住講:「活該。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 於是我們繼續走,約翰一路上偷笑著回家;然後他告訴了詹姆斯,詹姆斯笑著說:「活該。

passages.original: I knew that boy at school; he took great airs on himself because he was a farmer's son; he used to swagger about and bully the little boys.
passages.vernacular: 我喺學校認識嗰個男孩;佢因為係農夫嘅兒子,就擺大架子;佢常常大搖大擺,欺負小男孩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我在學校認識那個男孩;他因為是農夫的兒子,就擺大架子;他常常大搖大擺,欺負小男孩。

passages.original: Of course, we elder ones would not have any of that nonsense, and let him know that in the school and the playground farmers' sons and laborers' sons were all alike.
passages.vernacular: 當然,我哋年長嘅唔會容忍嗰種胡鬧,讓佢知道喺學校同操場上,農夫嘅兒子同工人嘅兒子都一樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然,我們年長的不會容忍那種胡鬧,讓他知道在學校和操場上,農夫的兒子和工人的兒子都一樣。

passages.original: I well remember one day, just before afternoon school, I found him at the large window catching flies and pulling off their wings.
passages.vernacular: 我清楚地記得有一天,就喺下午上課前,我發現佢喺大窗戶嗰度抓蒼蠅,扯掉佢哋嘅翅膀。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我清楚地記得有一天,就在下午上課前,我發現他在大窗戶那裡抓蒼蠅,扯掉它們的翅膀。

passages.original: He did not see me and I gave him a box on the ears that laid him sprawling on the floor.
passages.vernacular: 佢冇睇見我,我畀咗佢一記耳光,把佢打得四仰八叉倒喺地上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他沒看見我,我給了他一記耳光,把他打得四仰八叉倒在地上。

passages.original: Well, angry as I was, I was almost frightened, he roared and bellowed in such a style.
passages.vernacular: 嗯,雖然我好生氣,我幾乎被嚇到喇,佢嚎叫得咁厲害。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 嗯,雖然我很生氣,我幾乎被嚇到了,他嚎叫得那麼厲害。

passages.original: The boys rushed in from the playground, and the master ran in from the road to see who was being murdered.
passages.vernacular: 男孩哋從操場衝進嚟,老師從路上跑進嚟睇係邊個被謀殺喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 男孩們從操場衝進來,老師從路上跑進來看是誰被謀殺了。

passages.original: Of course I said fair and square at once what I had done, and why; then I showed the master the flies, some crushed and some crawling about helpless, and I showed him the wings on the window sill.
passages.vernacular: 當然我即刻老老實實講咗我做咗乜嘢,以及點解;然後我畀老師睇蒼蠅,有些被壓碎喇,有些無助地爬住,我還畀佢睇窗台上嘅翅膀。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 當然我立刻老老實實說了我做了什麼,以及為什麼;然後我給老師看蒼蠅,有些被壓碎了,有些無助地爬著,我還給他看窗台上的翅膀。

passages.original: I never saw him so angry before; but as Bill was still howling and whining, like the coward that he was, he did not give him any more punishment of that kind, but set him up on a stool for the rest of the afternoon, and said that he should not go out to play for that week.
passages.vernacular: 我從冇見佢咁生氣過;但係因為比爾仲喺像佢嗰樣嘅懦夫一樣號啕哀叫,佢冇再畀佢嗰種懲罰,而係讓佢坐喺凳子上度過下午剩下嘅時間,並講佢呢個星期不許出去玩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 我從沒見他那麼生氣過;但是因為比爾還在像他那樣的懦夫一樣號啕哀叫,他沒有再給他那種懲罰,而是讓他坐在凳子上度過下午剩下的時間,並說他這個星期不許出去玩。

passages.original: Then he talked to all the boys very seriously about cruelty, and said how hard-hearted and cowardly it was to hurt the weak and the helpless; but what stuck in my mind was this, he said that cruelty was the devil's own trade-mark, and if we saw any one who took pleasure in cruelty we might know who he belonged to, for the devil was a murderer from the beginning, and a tormentor to the end.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢好嚴肅地同所有男孩談咗殘忍,講傷害弱小無助嘅係幾咁鐵石心腸同懦弱;但留喺我心裡嘅係呢個,佢講殘忍係魔鬼嘅專屬商標,如果我哋睇見邊個以殘忍為樂,我哋就可以知道佢屬於邊個,因為魔鬼從起初就係兇手,到最後都係折磨者。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後他非常嚴肅地同所有男孩談了殘忍,說傷害弱小無助的是多麼鐵石心腸和懦弱;但留在我心裡的是這個,他說殘忍是魔鬼的專屬商標,如果我們看見誰以殘忍為樂,我們就可以知道他屬於誰,因為魔鬼從起初就是兇手,到最後也是折磨者。

passages.original: On the other hand, where we saw people who loved their neighbors, and were kind to man and beast, we might know that was God's mark.”
passages.vernacular: 另一方面,凡是我哋睇到愛鄰居、對人同獸都善良嘅人,我哋就可以知道嗰個係上帝嘅記號。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 另一方面,凡是我們看到愛鄰居、對人和獸都善良的人,我們就可以知道那是上帝的記號。」
